#788. Le Fée’s penalty stuns Chelsea and breathes life into defiant Sunderland

A lot can change in five‑and‑a‑half months, but as an early winter chill descended on Wearside last week – both meteorologically and ­metaphorically – Sunderland were determined that some things should remain the same. Just as they had beaten Chelsea on the final day of last season to ensure European qualification for the first time in 53 years, they did so again on Sunday to lift themselves off the bottom of the Premier League.

The Sunderland performance was certainly familiar to their head coach, Régis Le Bris – “the identity, the intensity, the togetherness, the way we managed the game” – on the way to three crucial points.

Ultimately a patched-up defence, ­without the injured Dan Ballard and the banned Omar Alderete, kept ­Chelsea at enough distance to allow Robin Roefs a tranquil ­afternoon amid the tumult. Chelsea may be ­developing into a ­chaotic must‑watch under Xabi Alonso but they were ­subdued here and have fallen out of the top four. “We didn’t produce enough to deserve to win,” Alonso said. “We lacked a bit of patience and creativity.”

Margins were paper-thin in a game decided by two first-half penalty calls, the first not awarded to Chelsea after Luke O’Nien’s clumsy challenge on Cole Palmer, deemed after video assistant referee consideration to be fractionally outside the area, and the second given to the hosts by Jarred Gillett after Levi Colwill brought down the ebullient Brian Brobbey; the defender argued, not without justification, that the Dutch striker had a handful of his shirt too but the award stood.

Alonso, as ever, made no excuses, ­focusing not on the officiating and more on how he was “not happy with how we defended that situation”. Enzo Le Fée had been equally unequi­vocal just beyond the half‑hour, sending Mike Penders the wrong way and dispatching into the goalkeeper’s bottom-right corner for the game’s only goal.

Europe may be a blessing for Sunderland but the full-time mood had been bleak after the latest alarming performance in the home defeat against Dinamo Zagreb on Thursday. It had felt like a season watershed and only the captain, Granit Xhaka, Thomas Meunier and Roefs survived the cull here. That the talismanic Xhaka, the subject of strong summer interest from his former coach Alonso, had his afternoon truncated by injury after less than three ­minutes, felt like yet more of the ill fortune dogging Sunderland.

There was no feeling sorry for themselves, though. With this the start of a challenging quartet of fixtures leading into the Tyne‑Wear derby next month, it felt like this match had to be attacked to prevent an early-season hiccup turning into a full mid‑season tangle with relegation trouble. And Chelsea were greeted with determination and ­aggression, with Xhaka’s withdrawal not ­blowing that plan off course. Two zesty ­incisions by Chemsdine Talbi in the opening quarter-hour, in his first ­Premier League start this season, caused Alonso’s men flutters, the first leading to a blocked Trai Hume shot and the second presenting Brobbey with a clear opening that he would have expected to convert.

The passion was there, the precision maybe less so. O’Nien’s challenge on Palmer elicited a penalty appeal that did not end up being costly after the VAR check and Morgan Rogers headed wide from a Marco Palestra cross, but Chelsea could not capitalise on any potential home nerves. If anyone was prone to belated Halloween frights it was the Blues, particularly at the hands of Brobbey, who led the line with enormous presence. He took on and beat the last man Wesley Fofana before steering his shot just too high, past Penders’ near post, and then won the penalty that led to Le Fée’s winner. “He is stoppable,” Alonso said, “but only when you defend better than we did.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Such was Chelsea’s bluntness in the first 45 that the coach opted for not just a substitution but a reshuffle at the break, with Estêvão replacing the injured Colwill, beefing up the attack with Moisés Caicedo slotting into the defence. Sunderland continued to fight tooth and nail in a game that threatened occasionally to bubble over. Meunier was booked for a late tackle on Caicedo and shortly afterwards Brobbey was cautioned for wrestling Roméo Lavia to the ground, a continuation of an ongoing feud between the pair. When he was substituted, spent, for the ­enduringly ­popular Wilson Isidor halfway through the second half Chelsea must have breathed a sigh of relief.

Estêvão made one burst through the middle on to a Rogers pass but Reinildo Mandava stepped across to snuff out the opportunity. Yet even with little possession Sunderland looked sharper. A ball broke for Isidor after Chelsea failed to clear Le Fée’s through ball, Penders saving and the rebound not breaking for the Frenchman before Pep Chavarría cleared.

As the last 10 minutes approached Alonso sent on Geovany Quenda for Chavarría, and the young winger finally conjured a goal attempt worthy of the description, fizzing a shot just wide of Roefs’s far post via deflection. Talbi, finishing as he started, pinged one just wide from distance on the break as the home side still looked more likely, even with a third of possession. Sunderland had rewarded their crowd’s vociferous faith.

#787. 'Tinkerman' Alonso's Chelsea side still searching for identity

Struggling Sunderland get a narrow win at home against Chelsea

Constant changes in formation and personnel - and another disappointing defeat.

Xabi Alonso's frustration was obvious as Chelsea's struggles for identity continued in the 1-0 defeat by Sunderland.

It is starting to feel as though the Spaniard is the latest "Tinkerman" at Stamford Bridge, a moniker first associated with Blues boss Claudio Ranieri back in 2002-03.

For the first time this season, Chelsea lined up with a three-man midfield - but they were also without a recognised striker for the second match in a row, with Pedro Neto again struggling to lead the line in their loss at the Stadium of Light.

By contrast, struggling Sunderland were led by target man Brian Brobbey, who won a 36th-minute penalty after being brought down by Levi Colwill. Enzo le Fee converted the game's only goal from the spot.

That decision came moments after Chelsea were denied a penalty when Cole Palmer went down under a challenge from Luke O'Nien, but the video assistant referee ruled that contact had started outside the box.

Those two incidents in quick succession meant Alonso and his coaching staff appeared angry on the touchline after the Sunderland goal.

However, the Chelsea manager refused to criticise the officials after the game - instead he gave brief answers that changed the subject and were critical towards his players for not carrying out the gameplan properly.

Asked whether Brobbey was simply unstoppable, Alonso, 44, replied: "No, he's stoppable. He's stoppable, but we have to do it better than we did today.

"Out of almost nothing he got a couple of chances. He got the penalty as well.

"I'm not happy with how we defended that situation. It's something that we could have avoided, something that we had worked on during the week. To concede penalties is not good for us."

It left nowhere to hide for Colwill, who was substituted at half-time, with Moises Caicedo filling in at centre-back despite having barely completed a full training session all week and needing careful management of his own fitness issues.

Chelsea also created few clear chances, aside from a headed opportunity that Â£117m signing Morgan Rogers squandered, while Palmer also struggled - days after being left out of the England squad.

Before the season started, Alonso said he wanted his Chelsea side to be "unpredictable".

Although factors such as injuries are beyond his control, his side have achieved that, but to their own detriment.

Failed to deal with Brobbey - player ratings for Sunderland v Chelsea

Sunderland beat Chelsea for first league win since August

Chelsea have five wins, four losses and a draw in 10 Premier League games under Xabi Alonso

Only Tottenham (28) have made more more line-up changes than Chelsea (24) in the Premier League this season.

In the early part of the campaign, they at least had a settled and exciting front three of Joao Pedro, Rogers and Palmer.

It was largely the reason behind the positive start to the season despite failing to keep a clean sheet against top-flight opposition until Alonso's eighth game in charge.

With Caicedo injured, they suffered problems in midfield and continued to make changes from match to match, while also experimenting with personnel to fix the defence.

However, they largely looked on course to emulate the back-three system Alonso excelled with during his historic German double-winning season at Bayer Leverkusen in 2023-24.

As Caicedo returned after the international break, however, captain Reece James was injured.

Joao Pedro featured in wins against Bournemouth and Everton before sustaining a thigh injury, having already missed Brazil's international matches.

Number one goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez broke his jaw in a collision at Everton, while Maxence Lacroix, who had been a near ever-present since joining from Crystal Palace in the summer, is expected to be out until January with a hamstring injury.

Defender Jorrel Hato has also suffered a setback in recent weeks.

It has left Alonso reacting to events when selecting his starting XI, with the Spaniard saying: "There are situations. Yesterday Josh [Acheampong] said he was not ready to play, so we are short of options and we need to walk through this step.

"Even when we win, when we lose, we miss some players that we have injured and for sure we are waiting for them to come back because they are important."

He admitted his side were missing Joao Pedro, although supporters have also been frustrated that Estevao Willian, who came on at half-time on Sunday, has started only one league match this season.

Prior to Sunday's game, Chelsea were averaging just 46% possession. They then dominated the ball at Sunderland (with 68.7% possession) but without creating many significant chances.

Meanwhile, only Crystal Palace have conceded more shots on target than Chelsea's 50, while the Blues top the league with 53 shots on target - meaning there have been plenty of chances at both ends during their matches.

Alonso can still be pleased with Chelsea having collected five more points than they managed from the equivalent fixtures last season, with the club on course to qualify for the Champions League while sitting fifth in the table.

However, that is a low bar after a dismal campaign last season, when Chelsea finished 10th.

Going into the November international break, Alonso remains a long way from establishing a style of play, or an identity capable of bringing consistency - although he promised promising in an interview last week that Chelsea would be "different" and "better" by the end of the season.

#786. Taylor Swift, Karlie Kloss Prove There's No Bad Blood at Chiefs Game

Taylor Swift and Karlie Kloss put feud rumors to rest as they cheered on the Kansas City Chiefs Nov. 8, just months after the supermodel attended the Grammy winner’s wedding to Travis Kelce.

If Taylor Swift and Karlie Kloss had problems, it looks like they were able to solve ‘em.

Four months after the model surprised fans with her attendance at the Grammy winner’s wedding to Travis Kelce, Swift and Kloss confirmed their friendship is far from ruined when they reunited at the Kansas City Chiefs game against the New York Jets at Arrowhead Stadium on Nov. 8.

To cheer on her guy on the Chiefs, Swift—who donned a striped red sweater—was joined in her suite by Kloss as well as her and Joshua Kushner's 5-year-old son Levi. Also stopping everything now to support Kelce were the "Opalite" singer’s parents Andrea Swift and Scott Swift, plus her mother-in-law Donna Kelce.

Swift, 36, and Kloss, 33, were all smiles as they supported the “Love Story” artist’s husband during his milestone 200th game in the NFL, with the pair even standing up to applaud and share a celebratory hug at one point, according to fan footage shared on social media.

And while Swift has been known to bring her celebrity pals to Chiefs games, including Tom Cruise and Caitlin Clark to name a few, her spending time with Kloss is particularly notable as they were rumored to have grown apart after being best friends in the mid 2010s.

Speculation surrounding their friendship began after the former Victoria’s Secret Angel’s name was noticeably left off a T-shirt that Swift wore in her 2017 music video for “Look What You Made Me Do”, which featured a list of her girl squad.

And though Kloss attempted to calm down the speculation by sharing a photo with Swift backstage at the Reputation tour in 2018, the “I Knew It, I Knew You” singer did not attend Kloss’ wedding to Kushner—with whom she also shares kids Elijah, 3, and Rae, 13 months—a few months later.

But the two seemingly confirmed that any past bad blood had been washed away when Kloss and her husband attended Swift and Kelce’s white veiled nuptials at New York City’s Madison Square Garden in July.

And just a few weeks after the star-studded occasion, Kloss appeared to prove all was well while shedding light on Swift’s special day.

For a closer look at Swift being a cheer captain at Chiefs games, keep reading...

While supporting Travis Kelce as the Kansas City Chiefs faced off against the Chicago Bears on Sept. 24, 2023, her first-ever NFL game at Arrowhead Stadium, Taylor Swift sported DÔEN's white Lois Tank and Ksubi's distressed denim shorts, which she paired with a Chiefs windbreaker and matching New Balance sneakers.

For the Chiefs' Oct. 1, 2023 game against the New York Jets, held at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, Swift wore Area denim shorts, which quickly sold out. The singer completed the look with Christian Louboutin boots and a relaxed leather shirt from Gant.

Of course, Swift didn't forget her signature red lip for the star-studded game, which was also attended by Blake Lively and Ryan Reynolds.

While spending time with father-in-law Ed Kelce at the Chiefs' Oct. 12, 2023 game, Swift wore a Chiefs jacket from WEAR, a line by Erin Andrews. The 'fit was, well, fitting since the sports reporter has been credited as the one who connected Swift with the guy on the Chiefs.

Swift, who also cheered alongside quarterback Patrick Mahomes' wife Brittany Mahomes at the game, chose a Balenciaga corset top to wear underneath the Chiefs jacket.

Swift had an extra special accessory on her wrist for the Chiefs' Oct. 22, 2023 game: An Erimish bracelet with Kelce's jersey number on it.

On Dec. 3, 2023, Swift sported a long red fleece jacket over a black high neck top, paired with her signature red lip.

The Grammy winner looked ecstatic as she played cheer captain with Mahomes.

In honor of Christmas,Swift donned a Santa hat with Kelce's jersey number during the Chiefs' Dec. 25, 2023 game against the Las Vegas Raiders.

For her ninth Chiefs game on Dec. 31, 2023, Swift sported a cream varsity jacket bearing the team's logo and a patch that read "Tay-Tay."

During a freezing January 2024 Kansas City Chiefs-Miami Dolphins game in Kansas City, Mo., Swift cheered on Kelce in a one-of-a kind puffer coat customized with his jersey number that was crafted by designer Kristin Juszczyk, the wife of San Francisco 49ers fullback Kyle Juszczyk.

Swift looked comfy and cozy in a sweater from Guest in Residence—the luxury cashmere brand founded by pal Gigi Hadid—as she snuggled up to Kelce following the Chiefs' AFC Championship win on Jan. 28, 2024.

The "Blank Space" artist wore a black Dion Lee crochet corset and Area crystal-slit jeans to the 2024 Super Bowl in Las Vegas, where she watched Kelce and the Chiefs beat out the San Francisco 49ers in a 25-22 game.

For the Chiefs' Sept. 5, 2024 home game—the first since their Super Bowl win—Swift rocked a Versace denim corset top, GRLFRND jean shorts from Revolve and thigh-high red latex boots. She completed the look with a Louis Vuitton handbag.

Swift wore an oversized tee as a dress with thigh-high boots during the Chiefs' Sept. 15, 2024 game against the Cincinnati Bengals.

On Oct. 7, 2024, Swift stepped out to the Chiefs' home game against the New Orleans Saints in a black-and-white plaid set from Vivienne Westwood and knee-high platform boots.

Swift attended the Chiefs' Nov. 10, 2024 home game against the Denver Broncos wearing a red and black tweed Versace blazer and skirt. She paired the pieces with a black Victoria’s Secret silk corset top, as well as a purse and knee-high boots from Versace.

Not quite an old cardigan, but Swift—strolling into Arrowhead Stadium with Travis' mom Donna Kelce and her dad Scott Swift—put her Louis Vuitton cashmere zip-up on to watch the Chiefs top the Raiders on Nov. 29, 2024.

Loving him was like dressing up in a Charlotte Simone coat and vintage Chanel hat to watch the Chiefs defeat the Houston Texans on Dec. 21, 2024.

After more than a fortnight away, Swift checked into Arrowhead for the AFC divisional playoff game Jan. 18, 2025 in head-to-toe Chanel and Canada Goose gloves.

Swift—arriving to watch the Chiefs take on the Buffalo Bills in the AFC championship game on Jan. 26, 2025—filled the blank space in her wardrobe with a complete Louis Vuitton look from boots to beanie.

While the Chiefs fell flat against the Philadelphia Eagles at the Feb. 29, 2025, Super Bowl in New Orleans, the singer made the whole Superdome shimmer in bedazzled denim shorts and a $1,300 Alaïa ribbed bodysuit.

For her first NFL game since marrying Kelce, Swift donned a red and cream gingham dress from Guest in Residence on Sept. 14, 2026.

Swift cheered on her guy on the Chiefs in a $39.99 tank top from WEAR by Erin Andrews, which she paired with light blue jeans, a black leather belt, a Cartier bracelet and a Catbird medallion necklace customized with Kelce's jersey number.

#785. Volkswagen logs Q3 operating loss of €5.86 billion on Porsche writedown

The Volkswagen Group has filed its worst quarterly performance since the height of the "Dieselgate" scandal in 2015. Share prices climbed in response, however, perhaps because the bad news was so well signposted.

The Volkswagen Group on Thursday posted its worst quarterly numbers in more than a decade.

The company reported an operating loss of €5.86 billion (roughly $6.53 billion) during July, August and September. One-off costs, not least a massive writedown in its stake in struggling sister company Porsche, explained the vast bulk of the losses.

The world's second-largest carmaker is battling mounting competition from and falling demand in the core Chinese market.

It is pursuing a major restructuring and downsizing program, trying to bolster falling profit margins, and executives said the difficulties highlighted the urgency of this process.

"The nine-month results make one thing clear: We cannot afford to lose any time. We must act quickly and decisively," chief financial officer Arno Antlitz said in a video statement.

The results were the latest reminder of the pressure on VW — and the wider German and Western automotive industry — to react to increasing competition in China, high costs and practical difficulties moving towards electric car production, and unpredictable and rising tariff burdens, thanks in no small part to US President Donald Trump.

And here are some of the key year-to-date 9-month figures:

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

VW shares were already at their lowest levels in well over 10 years prior to Thursday's announcements, after months of difficult headlines and the ongoing plans to shed tens of thousands of jobs and reduce production capacities.

Perhaps as a result of this, the stock dipped briefly as markets opened and the news was published, but then started to rally as the day progressed.

By midday in Frankfurt, VW shares had climbed by 2% compared to their prices at the start of trading on the DAX.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

CEO Oliver Blume plans to shed around 100,000 jobs across the group, which includes the Audi and Porsche brands, in the coming years though a combination of layoffs and not replacing departing or retiring personnel.

Multiple factors are contributing to this. They include increased competition from Chinese manufacturers, falling revenues in China, changeable US auto tariffs under President Donald Trump, different staffing requirements when manufacturing electric cars and difficulties moving towards making and selling more electric cars at the pace once designated by political leaders.

Up to four plants in Germany could face closure as part of the plan, which has met with considerable union resistance and could lead to strikes starting next year.

CFO Antlitz said the figures showed the urgency underlying these plans, saying the company needed to increase its profit margins by 2030 to solidify its finances.

Antlitz said the operating return on sales was only 3.8% in the first nine months of the year, even before the one-off writedowns hitting the bottom line.

"That is not enough in the long term," he said.

As part of its restructuring program, the VW Group aims to restore an operating profit margin of between 8-10% by 2030.

This year, amid one-off costs now totaling in the region of €10 billion, it expects a profit margin of no more than 1%, compared to prior forecasts in the region of 5%.

#784. Are 'outstanding' Brighton now Arsenal's main title challengers?

Brighton have won six of their last seven Premier League matches

Few, if any, Brighton supporters could have anticipated just how impressive their side would be during the opening 10 games of the Premier League season.

A 2-0 victory over Brentford at the Amex Stadium on Sunday afternoon lifted the Seagulls into second place, leaving them to head into the November international break dreaming of what might be possible over the remainder of the campaign.

Their sixth win in seven Premier League matches was enough to move them above Manchester City, who suffered a shock 3-1 defeat at Nottingham Forest less than 24 hours earlier, and underline their position as the closest challengers to leaders Arsenal.

With a five-point gap to the Gunners, that is certainly the case for now, although Brighton's influential midfielder Pascal Gross was reluctant to entertain such talk at this stage.

"No, we are not in a title race," the 35-year-old told Sky Sports after Sunday's success.

"But we have started the season really well. It's the beginning of the season.

"You see the Premier League, the margins and you look at the results - we are not getting carried away yet.

"Every game we have to suffer a lot. Sometimes it is momentum, but we are really pleased to head into the international break like this."

But 10 years on from Leicester City's title triumph against all odds, could they really achieve the impossible and win the Premier League?

Gross has made more than 290 appearances across two spells at Brighton

As each week passes, though, it is becoming increasingly difficult to dismiss Brighton's credentials.

Having won seven of their opening 10 Premier League matches, including beating Arsenal and Manchester City, the Seagulls have shown quality as well as character.

But it is not just their league position that makes for impressive reading. Almost all of the underlying numbers point to a side capable of maintaining their early-season form.

Brighton have created the second-highest number of big chances (37) in the division and scored more goals (26) than any other side this term.

Much of their attacking threat has been driven by Gross, who rejoined the club from Borussia Dortmund in January, having left in 2024.

The German midfielder has spent seven-and-a-half years at the Amex across two spells, either side of his spell back in his homeland, and has re-established himself as Brighton's creative heartbeat this season.

Gross has created eight big chances in the Premier League, more than any other player.

As well as finding the back of the net against Brentford, he also created at least five chances for his team-mates.

It was the 27th time since the start of the 2017-18 season that Gross has created five or more chances in a single match, with only Kevin de Bruyne (48) and Bruno Fernandes (47) having managed more.

He admitted earlier this week: "I just keep going. I think I'm fit, I try to prepare as good as I can and try to help the team win games."

At the other end of the pitch, only defending champions and current leaders Arsenal have been more impressive than Brighton, who have kept the joint-highest number of clean sheets (seven) and conceded the second-fewest goals (five) in the division.

"The way they're playing at the moment, Champions League qualification is probably the minimum that you'd expect Brighton to achieve," former Everton midfielder Leon Osman told BBC Sport.

"They look like a team that has really kicked on over the last 18 months. The football they're playing is outstanding and they are a great team to watch.

"Can they win the league? I think it would be unexpected if they did, but I expected them to win something this year, whether that is a domestic trophy like the FA Cup or the Conference League."

There was another welcome boost for Brighton as Yankuba Minteh made his first Premier League appearance of the season against Brentford.

The Gambia forward, who was the subject of an unsuccessful bid from Liverpool during the summer, has been one of their most dangerous attacking players since joining from Newcastle United in 2024.

Minteh's return to fitness is expected to be followed closely by that of Kaoru Mitoma, who has been sidelined since May with a hamstring complaint.

Arsenal have won nine of their 10 Premier League games this season, losing only to Brighton

There is a feeling an opportunity could be seized in the title race this season.

Although Arsenal have won nine of their opening 10 matches, they have arguably not been quite as convincing as they were during their title-winning campaign last season and were beaten 3-0 at Brighton in September.

Elsewhere, Manchester City fell further behind with a third successive league defeat on Saturday evening at the City Ground.

But even if Enzo Maresca's side were to rediscover their form after the international break - and visit Arsenal on 29 November - there remains considerable uncertainty over how their season could unfold following their financial charges.

City were found guilty of breaching 114 Premier League financial rules by an independent commission earlier this year, three-and-a-half years after they were first charged by the league.

The club have since exercised their right to appeal the verdict and vehemently deny any wrongdoing.

However, should they fail in their appeal, City could face a significant points deduction or, in the most extreme scenario, expulsion from the Premier League.

Were that to happen, Brighton would, based on the current standings, emerge as Arsenal's most realistic title challengers.

In fourth and fifth spot are Liverpool and Chelsea, the only two sides to have beaten Brighton in the league this season. But they appear to be enduring transitional campaigns and are currently a significant way off the pace required to mount a challenge.

Osman believed it was the perfect opportunity for Brighton to take advantage as he added: "They have taken time to build this team, letting some of their best players go and redoing the whole thing all over again.

"Now they just seem to be getting to a point where they'll be keeping their best players.

"They are in this great position where it is now time to get the most out of all this ability for their own success, to benefit the club and the fans, rather than just for the financial gain of selling players on for huge profits."

#783. Crystal Palace poised to sack Pierre Sage and target Frank after Liverpool defeat

Frenchman under pressure after four successive defeats

Former Spurs manager Frank emerging as main candidate

Crystal Palace are poised to sack Pierre Sage after Sunday’s defeat by Liverpool left them bottom of the Premier League for the first time since December 2017, with Thomas Frank emerging as the main candidate to succeed him.

The Frenchman, appointed in mid-June to replace Oliver Glasner, has been under mounting pressure since a 5-0 defeat by Brighton last month. There have been few signs of improvement as Palace have slumped to four successive league defeats.

Sage has guided Palace to only two wins from their 10 Premier League games this season and they have the league’s worst defensive record, with 24 goals conceded so far. Although there were promising moments during the 3-1 defeat by Liverpool at Selhurst Park on Sunday, their habit of conceding goals from set pieces has not been rectified and it is understood the patience of the club’s hierarchy has worn thin despite Sage only being at the helm for 16 matches.

He is expected to become the first Premier League manager to be sacked this season on Monday. Palace are already believed to have started the process of bringing in his replacement. Frank, who was dismissed by Tottenham in February, spoke to Palace in the summer and is said to be keen for a new challenge after a successful spell at Brentford.

The former Nottingham Forest manager Sean Dyche also has his backers at Palace and would be seen as a safe pair of hands given his vast experience in the Premier League. Vítor Pereira, another former Forest manager, could be an alternative.

Sage signed a three-year contract in south London after leaving Lens, where he won the Coupe de France and qualified for the Champions League in his final season. Palace have lost their two main central defenders this year, Marc Guéhi moving to Manchester City in January and Maxence Lacroix to Chelsea in the summer. Two loan players – Axel Disasi and the teenager Honest Ahanor – were signed as replacements. Palace did not land one of Sage’s top targets, Malick Fofana.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Sage denied after the Liverpool game that his dream job had turned into a “nightmare” but suggested that Palace’s squad needed investment in January. “We have to adjust some positions during the winter transfer window to give more solutions,” he said.

#782. Palace consider replacing Sage, with Frank among contenders

Liverpool dispatch Palace to pile pressure on Sage

Crystal Palace manager Pierre Sage is in serious danger of losing his job only five months into his reign, with the club bottom of the Premier League going into the international break.

Sunday's 3-1 defeat by Liverpool was Palace's fourth successive league loss, with Sage's side having won just two of their 10 league matches this season.

The club have held internal talks aimed at deciding Sage's future and his potential successor.

Former Tottenham and Brentford manager Thomas Frank is viewed as a strong candidate, while ex-Nottingham Forest boss Sean Dyche also has some support internally.

Both are out of work and would be available to start immediately.

Palace have taken just seven points from their 10 league matches and have the worst defensive record in the league, having conceded 24 goals.

They are also 21st in the Europa League, currently enough for a play-off spot, with only one win from their four matches.

If he is dismissed, Frenchman Sage could become the first managerial casualty of the Premier League season.

He was appointed on a three-year contract in June after Oliver Glasner departed at the end of last season.

"It's not from the dream to the nightmare," the 47-year-old said after the defeat by Liverpool.

"I'm not feeling this. I'm just in my job, and focusing on my job, and what I have to do to find the solution.

"The results are not at this level, and I know I have to push more on those things, especially in our way of playing, to make that move."

Sage previously led Lens to a second-place finish in Ligue 1 and a first French Cup triumph in their 120-year history.

However, he has been unable to replicate Glasner's success at Palace. Glasner, who now manages Nottingham Forest, led Palace to a first FA Cup title and a Europa Conference League triumph.

Palace are winless in the league since 11 October, with their losing run sparked by a 5-0 loss to fierce rivals Brighton.

After that match, Sage said he felt "shame" and admitted he did not know if he would be given time to turn Palace's fortunes around.

However, there was a degree of sympathy from some behind the scenes.

Injuries were not kind to his plans, while the absence of Jean-Philippe Mateta and Ismaila Sarr - due to a mixture of fitness and personal issues, related to both players' desire to leave the club - did not help the start of his reign.

However, three more league defeats have followed, with Palace hitting the bar and having a goal ruled out in their loss to Liverpool at Selhurst Park.

"We have to be more competitive," Sage said on Sunday.

"At the moment, we create some things, we expect a lot of things, but we don't have the results expected."

Palace's next Premier League match is at Coventry on 21 November following the two-week international break.

#781. What can you read into Premier League table after 10 games?

Only four teams have taken more points than Arsenal's 27 after 10 games

We are now more than a quarter of the way through the Premier League season, with each team having played 10 games.

History suggests the answer is quite a lot.

Last season, for instance, the top two - and two of the eventual bottom three - were in the exact spots at this stage that they in finished six months later.

How the Premier League table looks after 10 games

Arsenal are top of the table on 27 points - which is higher than the average number of points (23) champions have after 10 games.

In fact, only four teams have taken more points from their first 10 fixtures than the Gunners, and all four have gone on to win the league.

One small quirk that means Arenal fans should not start making plans for a parade just yet is that the only two previous sides to post exactly 27 points at this point of the campaign both failed to win the title - including the Gunners in 2022-23.

In 15 of the 34 Premier League seasons to date, the team top at this stage have gone on to win the title, so less than half the time.

While on 14 previous occasions, teams on 21 points, the tally of second-placed Brighton, or fewer after 10 games won the title, so there is still hope for the Seagulls.

However, the less good news for Fabian Hurzeler's side is that, bizarrely, the team in second after 10 games have won the title in just one of the past 18 seasons - that was Manchester City in 2022-23.

The fewest points any side has had at this stage and gone on to win the league is 18 - so City, on 21, and Liverpool, on 18, could still have a say.

Arsenal lead Brighton by five points, one fewer than the most points a team have ever come from behind at this stage to win a title.

Manchester United in 2002-03 and Manchester City in 2013-14 are the two to do that.

But Mikel Arteta and co can take comfort knowing the leaders at this stage have gone on to win the title in the past two seasons - after failing to do so in the previous four years.

Another 1-0 for relentless Arsenal - but did Odegaard spare VAR blushes?

Odegaard hits winner as Arsenal beat Hull to extend lead at top

Maresca's dream start turns into nightmare as title hopes hit

Crystal Palace are propping up the table having lost their past four league matches, but the stats suggest their position is far from terminal.

In total, 14 teams have stayed up having been bottom of the table at this point in the season - most recently Wolves in 2024-25.

Moreover, the fewest points a team has had after 10 games and stayed up at the end of the season is three.

That same Wolves team are the most recent of the four teams to have achieved that feat.

Sunderland, who climbed off the foot of the table with victory over Chelsea, had just four points at this stage in 2013-14 but still ended up finishing 14th.

Palace can also count themselves a little unfortunate to have amassed seven points and find themselves in 20th.

Only Bolton in 2002-03 have had more points (eight) after 10 games and been bottom - and that was in a situation when a number of other sides had played 11 matches.

Overall, 88 teams have previously had seven or fewer points after 10 Premier League games and 37 managed to stay up.

There is good news for Ipswich and Hull in that every promoted side since 2015-16 to take 11 points or more from their first 10 games - and there have been 14 of them - has survived.

The most recent promoted side to make as bright a start and go down were Cardiff in 2013-14, who were 12th with 12 points but finished bottom on 30 points.

The outlook is a little bleaker for Coventry.

Only two promoted sides in the past 11 seasons have taken fewer than 11 points and survived - Bournemouth in 2015-16 (eight) and Nottingham Forest in 2022-23 (five).

Frank Lampard's men are also the seventh promoted side to take exactly nine points from their first 10 games - two of the previous six survived (Wolves in 2009-10 and Leicester in 2014-15).

Lampard feels hair pull should have led to Coventry penalty

A long way to go then, still plenty of time for things to change. But how much do things really change from this point?

Well, not a great deal if we look at last season, when 15 of the 20 teams finished with three places of where they were after 10 games.

Aston Villa made the biggest jump, going from 11th at this stage to secure a top-four finish with time to spare.

So Champions League qualification remains well within grasp for Unai Emery's side, who are currently in 10th.

On the other extreme were Tottenham, riding high in sixth after 10 games before plummeting 11 places down the standings to finishing 17th, only securing survival on the final day.

As mentioned earlier, the top two and two of the eventual bottom three were already in their final positions by this point, while Burnley - the third relegated side - were only a place above the drop zone in 17th.

Perhaps Manchester United are in a relegation battle after all...?

#780. Jennifer Garner Details "Incredible" Chapter in Ben Affleck Marriage

Jennifer Garner pulled back the curtain on a sweet chapter during her marriage to Ben Affleck when she took the pair’s three kids on a European vacation: “It was wonderful.”

Jennifer Garner is thinking back to a time when she was thriving during her marriage to Ben Affleck.

The 13 Going on 30 alum detailed the unforgettable vacation she took with her and the Gone Girl star’s kids Violet, 20, Fin, 17, and Samuel, 14, before calling it quits with Affleck in 2015.

“When my kids were really little, I went to Paris,” Garner told Ina Garten on a recent episode of her Happy Hour podcast. “Ben was shooting some Batman-ish movie in London and we went for six weeks. I took them out of school. It was the last time I really took kids out of school, but it was wonderful. It was incredible. It was so fun.”

“And part of that is that we bopped around,” Garner recalled. “We went to Venice, we went to Paris.”

And while the Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice actor was busy getting into character as Bruce Wayne, it was Garten who suggested the Alias actress explore the French city by boat.

Since then, it’s turned into a full-blown tradition for the Daredevil actress. How fabulous is that?

“I’ve done it now, every time I go,” Garner said. “Every picture from that night, from that trip, the smile on my kids’ faces—it was such an adventure that you gave us.”

Garner and Affleck, both 54, tied the knot in 2005 before separating in 2015. And while they finalized their divorce in 2018, they’ve remained a team in co-parenting their little ones.

In fact, The Town actor recently gave his ex her flowers in the parenting department, calling her a “spectacular” mom on the Oct. 11 episode of Sunday Today with Willie Geist before admitting “it always makes me feel like I’m coming up a little short.”

And he’s not afraid to let his kids know that either, sharing he tells them that he’s “doing about 75 percent as good as your mom.”

“And they’re like, ‘Maybe 40 percent,’” he added with a laugh. “I’m maxing out. Woo, B+!”

But in all seriousness, Affleck expressed that he couldn’t be more “grateful” to have a co-parent like the Juno actress.

“I respect her,” he emphasized. “I think the most important thing is having that mutual respect—being able to get along with that person.”

Keep reading for more of Hollywood’s friendliest exes...

No, they are never, ever, ever getting back together. But at this point—between the birthday parties, the friendly embraces and even freaking acting out a sexual fantasy in a star-studded virtual reading of Fast Times at Ridgemont High—it feels like the former Hollywood golden couple is just taunting us.

You know you're cool when you can pop into your ex's talk show and give him a hard time. Such was the case when Silverman turned up on Kimmel's stage in 2018 to chat about her show I Love You, America and his "cute," "bright," "funny" wife Molly McNearney. "It's not fair!" the actress cracked. "She gets, like, new woke Jimmy. I had Man Show Jimmy."

TBH, we might still be mourning this relationship harder than either of its participants. Because when Faris—now married to cinematographer Michael Barrett—heard that Pratt was set to wed Katherine Schwarzenegger in 2019, she offered to officiate. She even sent over a gift after the newlyweds welcomed daughter Lyla in August 2020. Thrilled for son Jack to become a big brother, a source told E! News at the time that Faris "is very supportive."

It would have been super easy for the exes' relationship to become a flop. But more than four years after a messy split, the HGTV stars are still killing it at two projects: parenting kids Taylor and Brayden and turning run-down properties into someone else's dream home.

Literally "best friends" as the rocker put it in a 2013 interview with Oprah Winfrey, the parents to actress Zoe Kravitz still consider themselves kin. "We're one big happy family," Lenny said of his ex, who went on to wed Jason Momoa before their 2020 split. "It's beautiful, and it just shows you what can be done."

After the Dancing With the Stars co-host and former hockey player called in quits in 2020, the pair have continually proved they are on good terms.

In 2025, Hough enjoyed a trip to the lake with Laich and his then-pregnant fiancée Katrín Tanja Davíðsdóttir.

And when Laich announced his marriage to the former Crossfit athlete in 2025, Hough celebrated the news, writing on Instagram, “Congratulations! So so happy for you both. Sending you all the love, health and happiness for the years to come to you and your beautiful family."

Since their 2015 breakup, the parents to Violet, Seraphina and Samuel have hit the conscious uncoupling trifecta: Joint vacations, shared holidays and public displays of admiration with Ben dubbing his ex "an amazing mother" during a 2016 interview with E! News.

The Vampire Diaries costars may have called it quits in 2013 after three years of dating, but they've remained close friends since then. In 2014, somerhalder started dating Nikki Reed and tied the knot later that year. Naturally, Dobrev befriended the Twilight actress.

The two called it quits in July 2016 after five years together. The singer said on SiriusXM's The Howard Stern Show the following October that she's "very close" to Kinney, adding, "He's been my lover and a friend for so long."

"We love each other," she said. "That's it."

The Office's on-and-off pairing remained so tantalizingly close after the series wrapped in 2013 that even Kaling gets why people are still shipping them. Long the gold standard of copacetic exes, the parents to daughters Rumer, Tallulah and Scout remain so tight that the decision to ride out coronavirus stay-at-home orders together in Idaho was a no-brainer. Quarantine dance party anyone?

As for his relationship with Garth, he continued, "People come into your life for a reason and relationships can change," he told LaPalme. "Just because we aren't living together doesn't mean you can't love each other."

Despite a surprise separation in September 2012, the Blades of Glory costars decided to put on a united front for their children. "As you know, Will and I are very, very good friends," Poehler explained during a 2014 interview with Howard Stern. "We are doing a really good job. #779. ‘I expect to move forward’: Carrick denies risk of Manchester United sack

Bizarre 4-4 draw with Villa leaves United in bottom three

A tetchy Michael Carrick dismissed a suggestion he could resign as head coach for the good of the team after Sunday’s chaotic 4-4 draw with Aston Villa left Manchester United in the relegation zone heading into the international window.

Carrick’s side sit in 18th place with eight points from 10 games and have won only once, in August at home to Ipswich, in the league this season. It is now a club record eight Premier League games without a win.His job remains in the balance due to the dismal run of form.

Carrick was asked on Sky Sports if he was considering his position. “I’m not,” said the 45-year-old, who was curt when the interviewer said that it was clear there would be conversations regarding his future before United’s next game, which is away to Liverpool on 22 November.

“Is there?” he replied. “You’re telling me. I’m quite clear with what direction the club needs to go in, and it’s got to win games. #777. Germany seeks new head of state

The question of who should become Germany's new president is becoming pressing. Many want to see Germany's first female head of state. Chancellor Friedrich Merz is keeping his cards close to his chest.

Wanted: A new head of state — female, male, or other. Requirements: German citizen, entitled to vote, minimum age 40. Please apply as soon as possible! Availability starting January 30, 2027; job starts March 19, 2027.

This is not an official job posting, but Germany's federal government is indeed looking for someone to fill the nation's highest office. Having already served two terms, current President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is no longer eligible for another, leaving the position open for a successor. Many feel that it is time for Germany's first-ever female head of state.

"The person should have a certain level of public recognition, be politically unbiased, capable of bringing people together, approachable and a reasonably good [public] speaker," political scientist Ursula Münch told DW.

In Germany, a federal parliamentary republic, the president serves as head of state and a representative of the country as well as someone who embodies moral authority for the nation. Unlike in the US, France, or Russia, the president does not wield extensive political power or direct government affairs.

Steinmeier was nominated by his own party, the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), in 2009. However, once elected via a convention of parliamentarians and state electors, a president-elect has to suspend their party membership in order to serve in the office apolitically. This time, it is Chancellor Friedrich Merz's center-right Christian Democrats (CDU), the senior partner in the coalition government with the SPD and the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU), which has the right to nominate a candidate.

Political scientist Münch said that "the three parties must agree on a person who is acceptable for all three." Since the convention that will select Steinmeier's successor is currently controlled by these three parties and their delegates, it is very likely that whomever Merz nominates will be elected.

"Well, I would really like it to be a woman this time. We've had 12 male federal presidents since 1949 — it's about time for a woman. But if the right man were to be nominated, I'd be fine with that too," said Münch. According to an August survey conducted by the Forsa polling institute for the RTL television network, about 74% of German respondents say they don't care whether it's a man or a woman. Another 19% explicitly want a woman, while 5% prefer a man.

Ilse Aigner, president of the Bavarian State Parliament in Munich, appears to have a good chance. Aigner is a member of the smallest party in the coalition, the Bavarian CSU, and is considered a unifying figure. She also has experience in government in Berlin, having served as agricultural minister at the federal level. She enjoys strong support within her Bavarian CSU party, whose leader Markus Söder recently said: "It would be tremendous if she became federal president."

Even members of the opposition Greens and the SPD are full of praise for Aigner's candidacy. "What are we actually waiting for? Surely Ilse Aigner has long since secured a majority across party lines?" asked SPD parliamentary group leader Matthias Miersch recently. However, Merz, who is friends with Aigner, has remained tight-lipped so far — possibly also because Aigner is not a member of Merz's party, but rather of its smaller sister party, the CSU.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Other potential successors from the CDU membership have been mentioned: Bundestag President Julia Klöckner, former Defense Minister Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer and Education Minister Karin Prien. Hesse's state premier, Boris Rhein, is also a possible candidate. In recent days, another name has been making the rounds: lawyer Ines Claus, who serves as CDU's parliamentary group leader in Hesse and deputy party chair at the federal level — and is largely unknown.

However, rumors that she would be nominated were swiftly shot down by the chancellor. Sources close to Merz emphasized that he has so far "neither made a decision nor put forward a proposal." There are "a number of suitable" options, sources added.

The president is elected every five years by the Federal Convention, which comprises all 630 members of the Bundestag and an equal number of electors who represent the state parliaments. Among them are also prominent figures from the spheres of culture, science, sports and society. The candidate who receives more than 631 votes goes on to assume office. The governing parties — the CDU/CSU and the SPD — have a combined total of 682 votes, a comfortable majority.

The office of the president is often underestimated as merely a ceremonial role. Yet, as an authority standing above the political parties, this person wields considerable political, legal and moral influence. This is especially true in times of political polarization and international crises. While the president does not govern like a chancellor, he or she represents Germany both at home and abroad.

"From a constitutional perspective, the federal president is enormously important. For example, in a political crisis, he could decide whether it makes more sense to dissolve the Bundestag or to advocate for a minority government," explained political scientist Münch. In addition, he reviews and signs laws proposed by politicians.

The federal chancellor and CDU chairman has an interest in an orderly process, say sources close to the government. The "first milestone" will be the meetings of the CDU Presidium and Executive Board on November 9. Until then, discussions will be held with the state chairpersons of the CDU and the CSU. Sources made it clear that the SPD and the Greens will also be consulted, "since the election of the federal president should have broad support across the democratic spectrum."

That is how political scientist Münch sees it: "I still consider the question open, with a slight edge for CSU candidate Ilse Aigner." But there could still be a real surprise, she added.

#776. Bizarre & thrilling theatre as Carrick in limbo with Man Utd in drop zone

Man Utd score twice in stoppage-time to share points in eight-goal thriller

After yet another breathless, chaotic, shambolic Old Trafford classic, Manchester United do not know whether to laugh or cry.

Their fans didn't, booing at some points, cheering at others.

Defender Diogo Dalot was singled out for gruesome treatment amid the second-half protests and songs of defiance as he was replaced by Patrick Dorgu in the 66th minute.

The players didn't, running away joyously to celebrate Dorgu's 96th-minute equaliser that made it 4-4 against Aston Villa.

They then applauded the supporters who stayed on despite the apparent hopelessness of the situation as the game entered injury time with United trailing 4-2, presumably to vent their anger on a day when defeat seemed certain.

Manager Michael Carrick was in spiky mood when he was quizzed about his future by Sky Sports reporter Patrick Davison.

"That's not going to happen," he said, when asked if he was going to walk away.

"Will there?" Carrick then added, when it was suggested there would "clearly be conversations" with United's hierarchy.

"You're telling me what you think," he responded.

"I'm quite clear what direction the club needs to go in. It's got to win games."

Sunday's ridiculous eight-goal thriller with Villa - a game in which the hosts twice fought back from two goals down - left United in the drop zone in 18th place. Their lowest position for 40 years after playing at least 10 matches.

As they enter the international break, they will spend more time in the relegation zone than they have done since 1986.

United have not won a league game since they beat Ipswich on 30 August, have conceded 15 goals in their past five games and conceded inside two minutes in three of their past seven matches.

Three minutes and 40 seconds was the earliest they have ever trailed 2-0 in a Premier League game.

Up next is a trip to Anfield to play rivals Liverpool on 22 November.

On the positive side, United's players have not downed tools for their manager.

Somehow, despite being two goals down on three occasions in the past two games, they have emerged with a win and a draw.

Added to a creditable first-half display in a 2-0 loss at Chelsea on 31 October where they had Lisandro Martinez sent off, before which Carrick was backed to turn the current situation round, was that enough for Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazer family - and detached from this latest crazy day?

Was it enough for chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox who were at Old Trafford?

Four 'huge mistakes' that show Man Utd's defensive problems

Man Utd share 4-4 thriller with Villa but stay in drop zone

Dorgu makes dramatic impact - Man Utd v Aston Villa ratings

Carrick still in limbo & are Brighton title challengers?

Michael Carrick post-match interview - Manchester United v Aston Villa

"On the one hand it's dreadful to give up four goals at home," former United skipper Roy Keane told Sky Sports. "But they kept going, so you have to give them a little bit of praise.

"In terms of the bigger picture it's that rollercoaster of watching Manchester United. When you turn up most weeks there really is the feeling of not knowing what you're going to get."

Former United striker Dion Dublin offered his own take to BBC Sport, saying: "There's only so many times you can do that because it's quite tiring, physically and mentally. The players today were walking around after the game like they had lost, even though they got a point."

Some of the post-match interviews by United players backed up that observation.

"I don't feel happy - we are in a bad situation," admitted Dorgu. "We need to fight together to get out of it.

"Everyone needs to look at themselves and ask if they are doing enough. We need to fight for the manager, for the club and get out of this together."

The situation has not been made easier by fan sentiment.

Lack of form on the pitch, combined with the rising cost of ticket prices and a negative perception of how fans are being treated, has led to a negative reaction that is unprecedented in its ferocity since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013.

A banner was hung from the second tier of the Stretford End shortly before the teams came out to start the game. It read "We don't want a new stadium, we want new owners".

Full-back Dalot was jeered off the pitch when he was replaced by Dorgu, the catcalls replacing the cheers that greeted his number being shown.

Joshua Zirkzee, who scored United's third in the second minute of injury time, suffered similar treatment during a game against Newcastle almost two years ago. The Netherlands forward was still on the bench when Dalot arrived and offered his team-mate a consoling hug.

Aston Villa boss Unai Emery was livid by his side's late capitulation, which cost him a first victory at Old Trafford.

Touted as a potential successor to Carrick, he regathered his composure after storming down the tunnel before the final whistle to assure United fans the club's results will improve.

"They have the capacity, power, players and everything to overcome this situation," said the Spaniard.

That is probably true. But from so many angles, the current position remains grim.

The Villa game was like a number so far this season - Everton away, Atletico Madrid away, Tottenham at home, Leeds away, Chelsea away - where either United have played well, or got themselves into winning positions in stoppage time and failed to secure victory.

Although the present situation can still be rectified, it now needs two lots of results to go Carrick's way for the table to look more positive. Yet how long will it be before it is accepted that such anticipated improvement is not going to materialise?

Can United afford to wait until the January window opens? Have they got the resources to spend in it when it does?

These are bound to feed into the thinking of Ratcliffe, the Glazers, Berrada and Wilcox as they consider the future - plus the attractiveness of potential replacements.

For now, Carrick is still looking to a future he is certain will be brighter than what he has just endured.

"There's more than enough," he said, when asked if he had seen enough to believe the current situation can be improved.

"Goals change games and you've got to deal with it. It's something we have to improve on drastically. We're just making it too difficult for ourselves at certain times.

"[The players] are switched on and concentrated, it's a variety of things. There's not a theme to it, apart from these one-off moments are catching us out at the moment."

That’s not a problem. The only other person who’s been in and out of Skýborg wouldn’t datum when I hit her up. Least I think it’s a her. Could be that calling ID handle √^}° a ‘guerilla hat’ — all effect, no elegance — backfired, and I shouldn’t’ve pitched it as Us vs Them. But with less than a week between Skýborg getting decommissioned and the job coming in there wasn’t more time to nose around. Never got to the ransomware business, either.

Large black squares breach the snow after the trees clear out, all nine laid flat in the space of a football field. American. Tall stick figures cross the white and that’s my signal to play it cool. Trust the conditions. The C-Skin makes it easier — had it on since Reykjavík — and crossing the perimeter I go from blue-eyed, square-jawed Icelandic youth to ebony anthropoid, complete with pulsing orb in the forehead. Instant authentication.

Security for a decommissioned cloud data centre, that’s odd, right?

DC2 in leet — or (DC)2, if you’re an A-hat — Skýborg’s underground, and even from here it looks like those traceroutes were not a glitch. Place is up and active. What’s not active is this reindeer half buried in the snow, legs up, hole in its side. Poor guy got too close to security. The irony in that is that Sindri would’ve had a better chance of spotting my black hair through the nano-refraction.

My gear’s untraceable — I’m an A-hat at heart — and the only thing brought over is a foothold I left in the system, an hour of making the deal. By now everyone’s stuffing cred on the network so maybe someone’s found it … they haven’t. The rotors retract. I’m in. In cybersec, an unknown vulnerability is called a Zero-Day threat, something everyone worries about but never expects to walk through the front door. I take the stairs, just for laughs.

Think: you put your eggs in one place then pay someone else to hold the key. Asking for it, really.

Can’t blame these guys for wanting a bigger cut. Which, oddly, isn’t what they’re asking for. Not exactly. Either more than a little green, or it’s a joke. I mean, €12.49 to unfreeze the data? But in Nepalese currency? Or have you sit while they calculate the ransom value of π. My client’s in the clear — so far. Small fry, just wants the data stored here to disappear.

Speaking of here, it’s warm. Spidey sense going off at my level. Admin left in a hurry and dumped — dumped — some of the servers. But these are … moving? Ah, right. Wow. Server-drones. Didn’t think they were real. Mobilized. Security and storage. So not the normal stint of malware then. More like aware.

Which is something I’m still working on, haha. Thought-scanners can’t catch me while my THINKbox partitions the internal dialogue, or else I’d be a pulsing white spot. And reindeer. Speaking of spots … there’s my server. It’s easy once you’re in. Use the management console to turn on the identifier lights. Now: crowbar time.

Among hats, that’s a SEDkey. Does two things: secure erases the data then degausses the whole thing. Irreversible. Looks just like a key, too. Elegant enough for you, √^}°?

All these other drones are probably wondering why I’m getting so close. Anyway, key in and …

The three Americans currently living off Earth just made sure their electoral voices were heard.

Anil Menon told us today (Nov. 3) that he and fellow NASA astronauts Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins voted in the U.S. midterm elections from the International Space Station (ISS).

"Yes, you can even vote from space! All three U.S. crew members had the privilege of voting from space station. We filled out an electronic ballot and sent it securely to the election officials," Menon wrote in an X post this morning.

Yes, you can even vote from space! All three US crew members had the privilege of voting from space station. We filled out an electronic ballot and sent it securely to the election officials. https://t.co/hJCExQ2nKrNovember 3, 2026

That post included a 29-second video, in which Menon — wearing, like many of us today, an "I voted" sticker — shows us his "voting booth."

It's actually his room on the ISS, Menon explained. "Inside of it is my computer, where I was able to fill out an electronic form and send it to Harris County so I could vote today," he said.

Most NASA astronauts register to vote in Texas' Harris County; it's home to Johnson Space Center in Houston, the agency's human spaceflight hub.

Americans have been able to vote from space since 1997, when Texas passed a law allowing this to happen. The first person to take advantage of the legislation was NASA astronaut David Wolf, who cast his ballot from Russia's Mir space station that same year. (The ISS didn't welcome its first crew until November 2000.)

"Just like any other American away from home, astronauts may fill out a Federal Post Card Application to request an absentee ballot," NASA officials wrote in an astronaut-voting explainer.

The process is somewhat involved, however.

"After an astronaut fills out an electronic ballot aboard the orbiting laboratory, the document flows through NASA's Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System to a ground antenna at the agency's White Sands Test Facility in Las Cruces, New Mexico," they added. "From New Mexico, NASA transfers the ballot to the Mission Control Center at NASA Johnson and then on to the county clerk responsible for casting the ballot. To preserve the vote's integrity, the ballot is encrypted and accessible only by the astronaut and the clerk."

Delaney and Watkins launched to the ISS on Oct. 1 on SpaceX's Crew-13 mission. Menon has been there since mid-July, arriving aboard a Russian Soyuz spacecraft.

The trio currently share the orbiting lab with four other people — Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk and cosmonauts Anna Kikina, Pyotr Dubrov and Sergey Teteryatnikov. Kutryk and Teteryatnikov are members of Crew-13, whereas Dubrov and Kikina shared the Soyuz with Menon.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. "Little Red Dots are a hot topic in astronomy. You can compare studies to the tale of blind people who are trying to describe an elephant by touching it, and each person describes it differently based on what part they're touching."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

New research suggests that collisions between stars in the early universe were common, which could help explain the rapid growth of supermassive black holes and the existence of strange Little Red Dots seen by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST).

The team behind this research performed simulations of the early universe and found stellar systems were densely packed, leading to stars frequently slamming into each other. While rapid collisions would have destroyed the stars involved, slower collisions would have led to repeated mergers, creating single over-massive stars, which could collapse and form larger-than-usual black holes at the end of their lives. These could be the seeds of the first supermassive black holes.

Dense stellar environments do still exist in the modern universe at the hearts of galaxies; however, these aren't conducive to the types of collisions that would birth ultra-massive stars. That is because there are already supermassive black holes at the hearts of modern galaxies, and their immense gravitational influence speeds up orbiting stars, meaning collisions that do occur are high-speed and destructive, thus failing to birth overmassive stars.

"Perhaps the strangest outcome of our simulations is that stars can merge repeatedly within the cluster until they form one gigantic star with a mass equal to that of an entire cluster," team member Claire Williams, of the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), said in a statement. "When a star this huge reaches the end of its life, models suggest that it may have no option but to collapse into itself and form a massive black hole."

The existence of supermassive black holes before the universe was even 1 billion years old is something that has puzzled astronomers since the JWST started spotting them in 2022.

This is because black holes should need at least 1 billion years to complete the feeding and merger processes that result in a "supermassive" status of possessing millions or billions of times the mass of the sun. One suggestion put forward by scientists to explain this is that supermassive black holes don't start out from scratch. Instead, they form from black hole seeds called intermediate-mass black holes.

Normally, when a massive star collapses, it births a stellar-mass black hole possessing a mass between 10 and 100 times the mass of the sun. This is considerably smaller than supermassive black holes that dominate the hearts of all modern galaxies with masses millions to billions of times the mass of our star.

Intermediate-mass black holes are thought to sit between these two families of cosmic titans with masses between 100 and 100,000 times that of the sun. The problem is, no single star should have enough mass to collapse and create an intermediate-mass black hole. But that is valid only for the conditions we see in the "modern" 13.8-billion-year-old universe in our immediate cosmic vicinity. Conditions were very different further out into the universe and further back in time.

Indeed, such seeds emerged from these new simulations in environments of dense star clustering, which could solve this mystery by allowing those growth processes to get a head start.

"Dense star clusters provide a natural birthplace for massive black-hole seeds in our model," Williams said. "The same environment that forms the black hole can also provide stars and gas that influence its subsequent growth."

However, this could be a two-for-one deal. The JWST has also been routinely discovering astronomical bodies called Little Red Dots in the early universe. Little Red Dots are curious because they seem to have completely disappeared by the time the cosmos reached 2 billion years old.

Little Red Dots are extremely compact objects in the early universe that get their moniker from the fact that they look like red dots.

"Little Red Dots are a hot topic in astronomy. You can compare studies of people trying to understand Little Red Dots to the tale of blind people who are trying to describe an elephant by touching it, and each person describes it differently based on what part they’re touching," team member and UCLA researcher Smadar Naoz said. "Our research connects several of those perspectives together and may help us see more of the elephant."

There have been many suggestions about the true nature of these objects, but one theory suggests that they possess a rapidly growing black hole at their hearts.

The team's simulations suggest that Little Red Dots may be dense star clusters that are constantly being rocked by repeated stellar collisions. This results in a very large star, which eventually collapses to become an intermediate-mass black hole.But if that is the case, why were there no Little Red Dots around to celebrate the 2 billionth birthday of the universe?

Less than 1 billion years after the Big Bang, the universe was devoid of well-ordered spiral galaxies, but was instead filled with dense and chaotic clusters of star birth. As these regions were rocked with frequent star collisions, the conditions were right for ultra-massive stars to form and collapse into intermediate-mass black holes.

However, as the universe cooled and expanded, these sites became the building blocks of far less chaotic galaxies. Thus, if Little Red Dots are chaotic star clusters needed to form intermediate-mass black holes, progress toward an equilibrium state could explain why they suddenly disappeared from the universe. The cosmos just wasn't extreme enough to maintain Little Red Dots anymore.The team's research was published on Monday (Oct. 26) in the Astrophysical Journal.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. Follow him on Twitter @sciencef1rst.
