#770. Nick Jonas Details What He "Resents" About His Diabetes

Nick Jonas shed light on his decades-long journey with type 1 diabetes, revealing what he’s “grateful” for yet “resents” about the disease—which he was diagnosed with in 2005—in an open letter.

Nick Jonas is sharing insight into his health.

More than two decades after he was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes, the Jonas Brothers member detailed his complicated relationship with the disease in an open letter to his “old friend.”

“How long has it been? 21 years. 21 years, and you haven’t changed a bit,” Jonas wrote in the letter, which is a part of Dexcom’s A Letter to Diabetes initiative. “It’s funny how often we talk. Every few minutes, honestly. Staring at my phone to see where my glucose is. Reaching for my pump to bolus because I’m about to eat something with 17 carbs.”

“Those are just a couple of the hundreds of little decisions I make every week,” he continued. “Most people never notice them. But they add up to a real relationship, because that’s what diabetes is. It’s an ongoing conversation between your body, your mind, and your devices.”

The “Burnin’ Up” singer noted that there are days it feels like he and his condition are “on the same team,” while on others it seems like his diabetes is on a “solo mission.”

As Jonas—dad to daughter Malti, 4, with wife Priyanka Chopra—put it, “In a lot of ways, that’s what family is like. You rely on each other, you push each other, and you know they’ll always be there.”

But when the “A Little Bit Longer” artist was first diagnosed with diabetes in November 2005 at age 13, its “unpredictability threw” him for a loop.

“I’d built my whole life around this unrealistic structure and belief that I was in control,” he wrote. “You took that apart over the years, bit by bit. Part of me is grateful I learned that lesson. Part of me resents you for it. Full stop.”

Jonas then admitted, “There are days I wonder what life would feel like without you.”

That said, the Camp Rock star emphasized that being diagnosed with diabetes brought him something unexpected: a strong “community.”

“I always struggled to feel like I belonged anywhere,” Jonas recalled. “At school, I felt misunderstood. In most circles, for that matter. Through my childhood and youth, that was the theme. It wasn’t until I started talking openly about life with type 1, and meeting other people who were living it too, that I finally felt like I belonged somewhere.”

And while the “Jealous” singer “never wanted” to been painted as a “victim,” he continues to be open about his “truth” to help others feel “a little less alone.”

“I share my story for the 13-year-old who just got diagnosed and is lying in a hospital bed, scared to death,” Jonas noted. “I want them to be able to look up and see someone out there living their dreams while managing all of this, every single day.”

To see what other stars had to say about their journeys with diabetes, keep reading…

Nick Jonas can hit up the waffle house with an appetite and the know-how to manage his glucose levels.

The Jonas Brothers member has become one of the most high-profile stars with type 1 diabetes, with his diagnosis at 13 years old coming right before the sibling trio hit it big on the Disney Channel and with their 2006 debut album It's About Time.

Years later, Nick co-founded the nonprofit Beyond Type 1. Per its website, the organization “aims to change what it means to live with chronic illness” by “bridging the gap from diagnosis to cure, empowering people to live well today and funding a better tomorrow.”

Since his diagnosis, brothers Kevin and Joe have had Nick’s back as he monitors his health while keeping up with their rock-and-roll schedule.

“They’re incredibly supportive, and really help normalize it,” Nick explained to TODAY.com in 2023. “They understand that if I was irritable for an hour, that it’s probably because my glucose is high. And they give me grace, or make sure that if I’m starting to go low that I’ve got the juice I need or whatever at my disposal quickly.”

While a majority of people with type 1 diabetes are diagnosed in childhood, a stunned Lance Bass was in his 40s.

The *NSYNC singer detailed his diagnosis in a 2024 Instagram video, revealing he was previously misdiagnosed with type 2 diabetes, when in reality, he had developed type 1.5 diabetes.

Initially, "I had a difficult time getting my glucose levels under control, even though I made adjustments to my diet, my medications and my workout routine,” Lance said. “Things just weren't adding up.”

He now wears a Dexcom Continuous Glucose Monitor attached to his body. It takes readings of blood glucose levels every few minutes and sends alerts to a phone or receiver if it's changing rapidly so the person can potentially eat something carb-heavy if it's falling too fast or give themselves extra insulin if it's rising.

Meanwhile, Lance and husband Michael Turchin's twins, Alexander and Violet, 3, have taken an interest in his diabetes management routines as they play doctor at home.

"I'll show them the little needle that sticks out, and they just think it's fascinating," he said about his blood glucose monitor. “They're not scared of it at all. I explain over and over why I do this and what diabetes is, and you know, I don't know how much of that they're understanding. But you know, eventually they will."

Este Haim, seen above rocking her CGM while also rocking out onstage during a Haim concert alongside sisters Danielle Haim and Alana Haim, revealed how living with T1D has impacted her love life.

“I had a guy break up with me because I said that there was a possibility that our kid would have diabetes," she told British GQ in June 2025. "He was like, ‘Then why are we here?’ And I was like, ‘What?!'“

But it wasn’t the first time Haim endured disappointing reactions to her chronic illness, which she’s been navigating since her diagnosis at 14 years old.

“I was basically a social pariah for a very long time,” she told Beyond Type 1 in 2019. “You know, I was just the kid with diabetes in school that passes out and no one knows why and the girl with diabetes that smelled like orange juice all the time.”

Thankfully, like Nick Jonas, Este’s siblings have consistently shown up for her as she navigates tour life. “I’m lucky that I have Danielle and Alana to be my support," Haim said, "and when I am having a bad day, a bad week, a bad month, they’re always the first people to be like, ‘Dude we got you. Whatever you need. We’re going to get through this. Let’s get you a healthy meal. Let’s not have pizza after the show tonight. Let’s go get you something good so that you don’t wake up and your blood sugar is 350.’”

Bret Michaels has detailed the thorns poking out of his rosy career.

In a June 2025 Instagram post, the Poison frontman explained how living with type 1 diabetes might impact his tour schedule after a health scare.

“Unfortunately, the highs and lows of living with diabetes since I've been six years old occasionally just kick my butt,” Michaels wrote. “Last night, I went on stage and even added a song or two to the set to prove to myself & the fans that I could do it. At the end, my blood sugar walking off the stage was a real-life 39.”

Per the CDC, 70 mg / dL is considered low blood sugar for people with T1D—and severe low blood sugar begins at 54 mg / dL.

“I vow in the near future, I'm going to take that time needed,” he told fans. “And please forgive me if I have to move some of the shows around until I get this under control.

That’s not to say, Michaels hasn’t taken plenty of precautions along his decades-spanning career.

"I wake up and the first thing I do is check my constant glucose monitor," Michaels told People in 2024. "I take an injection and then the next thing I do is I get up and—good, bad or indifferent, no matter how I'm feeling—I get into a workout routine, and it helps to level the blood sugar out.”

He added, "And then I jump into the fun and the business of the day, and just try to take every day like that."

John Legend and Chrissy Teigen's son Miles

John Legend and Chrissy Teigen are proving to be extraordinary people when it comes to their son Miles' type 1 diagnosis.

The Cravings cookbook author detailed their shock upon discovering his T1D status on, after Miles was hospitalized for an unrelated health issue. “I've learned since then that this is how so many young children end up being diagnosed with type-1," she wrote on Instagram in July 2024, "going to the hospital for something completely different."

Teigen—also mom to Lunda, Esti and Wren—later shared how this inspired her to become an advocate with advanced screening for T1D. “I was blown away by the fact that not only did I not know that screening was an option when I first had children—I have four kids by the way—I didn’t hear about early screening at any point during any of my pregnancies,” she said at the Women’s Health Lab panel in May 2025. “It would’ve made an incredible amount of difference.”

The Dancing With the Stars pro shared her Type 1 diabetes diagnosis in May 2024, and has since been open about the strength she's earned through her experience.

“It’s a hard diagnosis and it takes a lot of time and just thinking out of your life, but I think it’s made me stronger and more mature,” she told Woman’s World in a July 2025 interview. “I’m able to handle conflict and hard things in my life better, because I go through the management and just the hard things that come with type one diabetes.”

Plus, she added, “It brings me so much motivation every day, because I want to be an inspiration to others. I want to be an inspiration to young people or anyone with [any] type of diabetes, so if it really gives me that motivation every day that I’m doing it for them and not just for myself.”

Hoda Kotb got some breaking news about her daughter Hope in 2023.

Yet, the former Today anchor waited until after she left the morning show full-time to reveal her youngest child was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes.

“Hope is fine for most of the day. There are just moments where you have to watch her," she told former cohosts Craig Melvin and Savannah Guthrie when returning to Studio 1A in May 2025. "I was totaling it up—five minutes at breakfast, five minutes at lunch, five minutes at dinner, sometimes overnight. Add that up, that's a half-hour.”

“So, for 23 and a half hours,” Kotb added. “She's every other kid. So, I try to remember that."

Kate Moss' model daughter Lila Moss celebrated the debut of some diabetes-chic accessories made for a groundbreaking Barbie.

A continuous glucose monitor and insulin pump are signature features of Mattel’s first-ever doll with type 1 diabetes. As the company noted in a July 2025 statement, its collaboration with Breakthrough T1D was "designed with inclusion and empathy at the core."

To celebrate the release, Mattel honored two type 1 diabetes ambassadors, Peloton instructor Robin Arzón and Moss, presenting them with their own one-of-a-kind dolls.

Upon the Barbie’s reveal, Moss wrote on Instagram, "This has been such a special project to be a part of, I hope this can encourage anyone living with Type 1 to not be afraid of wearing their pump proudly and that it helps to raise awareness on why we have them and what they do for us!"

It's not the first time that NASA has considered sending a robotic spacecraft to help Hubble.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA is reviving discussions to rescue the Hubble Space Telescope, which is operating well but is on track to reenter Earth's atmosphere about six years from now.

The agency issued a request for information (RFI) on Oct. 29 for "in-space servicing" capabilities, which could include boosting Hubble's orbit (which is naturally degrading due to atmospheric drag), or even a mission to "enhance its capabilities" in some way.

Hubble, which launched in April 1990 in partnership with the European Space Agency, was serviced five times by astronauts on space shuttle missions, the most recent being in 2009. The observatory's groundbreaking achievements include helping to show that the expansion of the universe is accelerating — a discovery that won the Nobel Prize — as well as a swath of finds about planets, galaxies, stars and other parts of the universe.

Hubble also regularly teams up with other telescopes for science work, and its observations have led to the publication of at least 23,000 scientific papers, NASA figures suggest. And, despite its age, Hubble remains in high demand. "Astronomers request about seven times as much observing time as is available each year," the agency stated in September.

Hubble is also widely appreciated by the public. People have long enjoyed and celebrated its iconic images, such as the Eagle Nebula's "Pillars of Creation," a gorgeous shot that has been revisited several times over the decades. As such, this is not the first time in recent years that discussions have opened about keeping the famed observatory running for a while longer.

In 2022, for example, billionaire tech entrepreneur Jared Isaacman proposed using SpaceX hardware to mount a Hubble-servicing mission. (Isaacman also purchased and commanded two crewed SpaceX missions to Earth orbit, which flew in September 2021 and September 2024.) NASA declined, however, citing possible risks to the healthy observatory.

But things have changed, apparently. Isaacman, who in December 2025 became NASA administrator, said in an Oct. 30 agency statement that Hubble's science return means the agency should "be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible" — especially if doing so would be a cost savings compared with launching another mission.

In an Oct. 30 post on X, Isaacman added that it's "still worth exploring the options" and noted that NASA had previously considered "a far lower-cost solution" to keep the observatory flying. "That was then. Still worth the effort — Hubble deserves it," he added.

The new RFI also allows for alternative scenarios, however, which could include a "safe, controlled reentry into Earth's atmosphere or orbital disposal at the end of Hubble's mission."

Hubble will naturally enter the atmosphere in 2033 or 2034 due to orbital drag, so any attempt to service it would have to be in 2032, the agency stated.

Earlier this year, NASA worked with Katalyst Space Technologies on a $30 million mission that aimed to boost the orbit of the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, which is also falling back to Earth due to orbital drag.

That long-shot rescue mission — which was developed quickly to race against accelerated solar activity, which ballooned Earth's atmosphere and increased drag — launched successfully this summer. But control issues prevented Katalyst's LINK spacecraft from meeting up with Swift. Swift is expected to reenter Earth's atmosphere tomorrow (Nov. 4) after 22 years of operations — far past its two-year design lifetime.

Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

#767. Love Is Blind’s Rob Reveals What You Didn’t See Before His Crash Out

Love Is Blind season 11 contestant Rob Feeley exclusively told E! News about what led to his on-camera meltdown after speaking with pod mate Diana Perrone.

Rob Feeley is shedding light on what set him off on Love Is Blind.

The season 11 star finally explained why he had a meltdown at a group mixer after speaking with castmate and ex Diana Perrone, shouting that he was going to be "cancelled" following their conversation, which was largely unaired.

According to Rob, he didn't think it was necessary for him to sit down with her in the first place, since he was attending the St. Patrick's Day party with fiancée Michaella Giorgio.

"When I go in with Michaela, I don't need to see another girl," Rob told E! News in an exclusive interview. "I don't need to see these people. I don't need to have a conversation with Diana. We ended in the pods respectfully. I think she might have even got engaged herself at some point after."

"It's Michaella I care about," the 40-year-old continued. "I just thought it was inappropriate to put me at a table and try to speak to [Diana]. We had closure."

After their conversation, Rob appeared to become paranoid about their sit-down, shouting in the scene that Netflix was "gonna manipulate this whole thing into something crazy. I don’t give a f--k."

"I don't need to be put in the situation where I have to speak to somebody who I dated in a pod, because I chose Michaella," he told E!. "It wasn't anything where I had something specific to say to Diana."

He added, "It was more respecting Michaella than it was anything else."

Ultimately, the AI software salesman said the pressure of being on a reality TV show got "so immense" for him, resulting in his breakdowns both at the group mixer and at a bar with friends.

"It's just a lot of pressure, and I didn't know how to deal with the pressure," he explained. "I probably wasn't in the right mindset going in with some other things I experienced. Not a crutch by any means, but I tried to look past that. And when it came down to it, I just felt like maybe this isn't for me."

As he put it, "I didn't handle it the best, and I just felt like all the pressure just got to me, the filming, and I just cracked."

After Rob and Michaella broke up and filming wrapped, Rob said he spent 50 days focusing on himself—"no drinks, just work"—and 75 days of "eating right, no cheat meals," as well as getting therapy and doing cold plunges.

"I acted not in character," he added of his time on Love Is Blind. "That's not really who I am. Those couple scenes weren't who I am. I don't want to blame production. I don't want to blame anybody but myself."

For a check in on where other couples stand, read on.

Though yacht captain Blake’s romance with marketing manager Erika appeared to be smooth sailing after the pods, just one week before their wedding, the couple realized they may be in too deep due to their dramatically different lifestyles.

“I don’t want to hold you back,” Blake told Erika during the season 11 finale. “I don’t want you to be that captain’s wife on the widow walk. I don’t want to marry you and then for you to feel held hostage while I’m sailing around, gone for weeks on end. And then you’ve got a timeline with kids and everything.”

“I just think at this point, there’s too many concerns, too many questions that I can’t say yes at the altar,” she shared. “I just think the best thing to do is to leave the experiment.”

And while Erika cried over their decision, Blake had already concluded their ship had sailed.

“The experiment is done, but it’s the right move,” Blake confirmed. And when a producer asked if he ever had a love like this, he replied: “I’m not gonna answer that one…I’m feeling a little relieved, a little exhausted.”

While both Wilson and Wilnie had the times of their lives at their respective bachelor and bachelorette celebrations, the party was definitely over before they reached the altar.

In fact, they couldn’t see eye-to-eye on life's more mundane tasks, including dividing up cooking duties and household chores.

“When we got out of the pods, you got everything I promised you, plus,” Wilson told Wilnie following an off-camera disagreement, later adding, “You said it countless times, ‘I’ll do the things for you that make you happy.’ And I’ve mentioned what those things might be, but then you’ll be like, ‘But I don’t like doing that…I’m not used to doing that.’”

As for Wilnie, she couldn’t disagree more. “I don’t work in the home,” the mental health counselor explained. “I have long, emotionally draining days and whether you agree with that, when I get home, it is hard for me to always be at your level.”

Ultimately, for Wilson, there were too many issues at hand for them to tie the knot. “It’s not that you’re a bad person,” the senior compliance manager shared, “you’re a phenomenal person but maybe marriage is not for us.”

By the end, though a tearful Wilnie confirmed she still loved Wilson, she doesn’t regret their path.

Cam Halloran & Aneha Singh: To Be Determined

Once Aneha and Cam entered the real world, her hesitation to marry someone with a different background and religious beliefs —especially in the wake of her family’s disapproval—and their communication skills proved to be hurdles. And, yet, they seemed determined to scale them together.

However, once asked whether she was ready to say “I do,” the principal engineer shared that she couldn’t, telling her fiancé: “I still believe you’re my person, but I do not today. I need more time.”

As for Cam, he assured her that he completely understood. “It’s okay,” the human resource coordinator replied. “it’s a big decision. I feel like we both need to be one hundred percent confident.”

But once Aneha declared she didn’t and danced away from the altar while stressing to Cam that he was still her fiancé, he teared up watching her leave. As he later explained to his family, he simply didn’t “know what happens now.”

Shortly after, Aneha and Cam did end up meeting up one final time. And while Cam expressed that he still loved and cared for her, he needed time to process the “I don’t” of it all.

When healthcare worker Sarah started to fall for account executive John, they initially disagreed on fundamental topics such as abortion rights and vaccinations. However, despite their perspectives, they both said yes to spending their lives together, becoming the only couple to get married during the show’s 11th season.

“It’s fun looking back on the first few days ‘cause I don’t think we liked each other very much,” she shared. “And then, some people here heard the story about you maybe not being too jazzed to keep talking to me. But I love that that happened, because I think that was a catalyst for us.”

She noted, “After that, I’ve never been so sure on someone, and I had never even seen you. And then when I saw you, I felt like I’d already known you a lifetime.”

Just before the season's reunion aired, however, court documents showed Sarah filed for divorce just over a year after they tied the knot.

Even though the pair were shaping up to be frontrunners once they left the pods, Rob and Michaella’s relationship came to a screeching halt after he had two shocking public outbursts during episode 10.

After a hangout with his fellow friends went left once a bartender cut one of them off, Rob then came to the cast meet-up with another bone to pick.

"I’m going down in this thing as the biggest piece of s--t,” he yelled at the bar. “Right where Netflix wants me, buddy. Dude, they’re gonna manipulate this whole thing into something crazy. I don’t give a f--k."

In fact, his behavior amongst his castmates—in addition to other uncomfortable moments between the two of them—made Michaella think twice about completing the rest of their journey.

"I don’t deserve any of what I’m getting," she expressed through tears. "I love him. It’s just a lot. And we’re not getting married. I cannot marry this man under any circumstances."

Scott “Stew” Stewart & Jacqueline “Jax” Guelli: Split

Despite their initial chemistry in the pods, Stew and Jax fizzled out almost immediately once they met face-to-face.

However, even after ending their engagement, they’ve coming to a crystal-clear understanding as friends. In fact, Stew shared that even though Jax had turned down producers’ offer to meet up again immediately after their reveal, she then reached out on her own terms.

"It was super sincere," he previously told E! News. "She explained that it wasn't about me. It was about just the emotional overload of the previous couple weeks, and I think once we got settled back in Boston, once kind of normal life was allowed to resume, we were able to kind of catch our breaths."

Heading into their big day, Amber—who is mom to daughter Emma—expressed worry over Jordan actually saying “I do” when it came time.

But, her fears were put to rest as the two both ended up saying yes, leaving almost everyone present to shed tears, including her daughter.

However, their relationship came to an end just four months later, the former couple revealed during an emotional face-off at the March 2026 season 10 reunion.

Brittany Wicker & Devonta Anderson: Split

Right before their nuptials, season 10's Brittany revealed she was “shocked” when Devonta called it all off.

“Today was supposed to be our wedding day but it’s not,” she told the camera. “But right now, I feel like everything I want isn’t happening.”

As for her now ex, though Devonta noted that everything between then was “great,” ultimately, “I can’t walk into a marriage with self-doubt of ‘Can I love you how you need to be loved?’ I think that’s why I couldn’t get to the altar. I just can’t do it.”

And though Brittany walked away noting that they’re “still going to be together,” Devonta confirmed he’s not on the same page.

Indeed, Devonta revealed at the March 2026 reunion that he is now engaged to an old friend and the two are expecting a baby. The pair welcomed son Kyler Lee Anderson in August 2026.

Brianna “Breezy” McNees & Connor Spies: Split

Though season 10 star Bri decided she and Connor weren’t ready to get married just days before their wedding, at the show’s March 2026 reunion, the pair confirmed they’re still very much in love and working on eventually getting to their happily ever after.

But their journey reached a hard stop weeks later, Connor sharing on the Table for 1 podcast in June, "I'm not dating Bri anymore."

The season 10 couple's engagement came to an abrupt end once Chris confessed to Jessica that he wasn't physically attracted to her.

However, Jessica has since found love in another pod mate, as she revealed at the March 2026 reunion, with fellow doctor Haramol Gill.

"You are everything, Jess," Haramol told her during the special. "Every room you walk into gets brighter."

Though the season 10 pair nearly exchanged vows after falling in love sight unseen, their differing perspectives on having kids—Emma has voiced her uncertainty while Mike has been firm about having them—was too much of a factor to compromise on.

“I do love you,” Mike told Emma. “Right now, I’m not ready to say I do. I want kids. And I want to know that you definitely, 100 percent want a family with me. I don’t wanna say yes and jump into something and then it changes down the road.”

And though Emma noted she can “see glimpses of a family,” in their future, Mike shared that he wants to her to be certain.

"If we’re gonna get married, I want you to know that you want a family with me for sure,” he explained. “I don’t want it to be half-ass…And you have your reasons and I respect them and respect them but I just can’t say yes without knowing that. So, I’m sorry."

Mike has since hard-launched a new romance.

Before walking down the aisle in the season 10 finale, the soccer coach compared his wedding day to a “penalty shootout with everything on the line,” noting that he was confident that they would make it.

However, Ashley made it clear that it wouldn’t be the goal and jumped in when he was presented with whether he would say “I do.”

"I know what you’re going to say," she told him. "I know you don’t choose me and I’m not choosing you either.” Ashley went on to list a number of reasons why they didn’t work out, including questions about his integrity. A point Alex made sure to address in that very same moment.

"I do disagree to an extent about the integrity," he told her. "I felt as though the questions about my past were more to try and catch me in something than really understand me."

And if you’re wondering whether he would do anything differently: "Absolutely no regrets on my end, I’m so pleased and proud of myself as a person."

Victor "Vic" St. John & Christine Hamilton: Married

From the start of season 10, Christine and Vic were instantly a match made in pod heaven, with the two both happily agreeing to their future together.

"I never thought I would fall in love in such a unique experiment, and Christine,” he noted during his vows, “the moment we spoke in those pods, we just connected…You know more about me than anyone else on this planet."

She marked his 35th birthday in September with an Instagram tribute to "the kindest, most hardworking, humble, strong, gentle, passionate, joyful, God-fearing man."

In the end, Anton's drinking habits and financial situation didn't seem to match what Ali was seeking.

"I can't be your wife," she told the truck driver at the altar in season nine. "The person I fell in love with in the pods isn't the person I've gotten to experience in real life."

"It just didn't feel right or how I would expect that moment to feel like," she told the cameras. "I don't feel he was super forthcoming about his lifestyle."

Anton's reaction? "I don't know if it's looks, I don't know if it's the vibes or I don't know if it's the way that we were living together. But I can say I've done nothing but care for her."

Though the couple bonded over having loved ones with Type 1 diabetes, their differing lifestyles (he preferred a more simplistic way of life; she loves luxury) were a breaking point for Megan, who called off the wedding at the end of the season nine finale.

"We're ships in the night, like two different people," the entrepreneur told him. But the metaphor passed him by, with Jordan insisting, "I don't see it."

When Megan cited his picky eating habits and his inflexible travel schedule as a dad, Jordan told her, "I don't know why you chose me in the pods then."

"Initially I leaned into opposites attract but I still just have reservations," she explained before they each began crying. "Knowing this today, there's no way I wanted to go to the altar and put either of us through that."

Jordan shared his one regret was introducing her to his son, Luca, saying in a confessional, "I feel like she doesn't love me for me and that's the closure I need."

Megan admitted the ordeal had her "questioning if I'm even cut out to be a mom. Maybe I am too caught up in my own life."

But at the October 2025 reunion, she revealed she and partner Paul Wegman had welcomed a son they named Brooks.

Kalybriah Haskin & Edmond L. Harvey: Split

They both confessed they "love the hell out of" each other at the altar, but season nine's Kalybriah turned Edmond down with an apology.

"You deserve someone that is 100 percent at the altar and I'm not 100 percent right now," she told the realtor. Still, she stressed, "My no doesn't mean that I don't love you."

While Edmond broke down in tears, Kalybriah thanked him for being "so graceful" as she made the "hard" decision. When he asked if she'd date him "down the road," Kalybriah said she'd never write him off.

"I am shocked," he said in a confessional of her decision. "There was no bright side."

The pair didn't make it to the altar in season nine, as Joe ended the relationship after having a breakdown at his tux fitting.

"I kind of dug deeper, like, 'What is your typical type?' And he was like, 'I just usually date more petite women,'" she recalled to the outlet. "I am a really confident person. At that moment, it kind of put me into this insecure feeling."

Joe defended his comment, telling the outlet, “I was trying, poorly, to explain a pattern in my past dating experiences, not to compare or criticize."

Nick dumped Annie before the wedding day in season nine, explaining he was hurt that she continued to say she loved him more than he loved her.

However, the hairstylist refused to believe it was over and tried to convince Nick to continue, saying, "Just be in this and love me."

Lauren O'Brien and David Bettenburg: Split

Not to mention, Dave also didn’t want to introduce Lauren to his friends and family, noting that his dad didn’t know of his engagement and that his sister—who became a big point of contention—disapproved of their relationship altogether.

One of the most compatible couples of season eight, most viewers assumed Monica and Joey would make it down the aisle and beyond. However, when it came to saying "I do," Monica instead said, "I don’t right now."

"In this moment, it's 100 percent," she said through tears, "and I just feel like we're both, we're not quite there." As for Joey, he agreed with every word.

And I agree, I don’t think I would be ready. And to be completely honest, I’m also not 100 percent at this time.”

Though season eight's Ben and Sara seemed to disagree on major components of their life together—including religion and politics—by wedding day, the pair seemed to have gotten on the same page. But ultimately, they decided to end their shared story.

As Sara—who said, "I don’t" to a future with Ben—explained, "Ben, I love you so much but I always wanted a partner to be on the same wavelength, and so today, I can't. I'm sorry but I don't want that to be misunderstood."

Another season eight couple who seemed to be focused on the road ahead post-pods, Devin and Virginia, got along perfectly fine—that is, until the topic of having a prenup came up.

“I think that in a lot of our relationship, I wanted to protect Devin,” she said, through tears, after the leaving the altar. “And I don't know if that's a cultural thing, but it's always been important for me to protect him. So there was just depths of our relationship that we didn't get to. We just didn't get there.”

There was at least one season eight couple who did say yes to a season of love past Christmas.

Though the pair seemed to face quite the hurdle (Taylor was convinced Daniel followed, then unfollowed her on Instagram before the show and therefore, knew what she looked like), they managed to clear that particular obstacle.

In fact, after exchanging emotional vows, the two enjoyed a beautiful wedding and celebratory reception.

"We did it," Daniel said while sitting alongisde Taylor after their nuptials, with Taylor adding, "We're so excited to start the next chapter." They marked two years of their "wild journey" with a March 2026 Instagram post.

Brittany Wisniewski and Leo Braudy: Split

Though the now-famed art dealer decided to pop the question to the Keeping Well author following his season seven love triangle with Hannah Jiles, the pair ultimately decided after their short engagement, they were better off as friends.

We're very good communicators, so it was not a big ordeal. It was a very clean, respectful realization.”

Shortly after her appearance on the Netflix dating show, Brittany debuted her romance with musician Mod Sun in November 2024, but she confirmed in July 2025 that the pair had called it quits.

Monica Davis and Stephen Richardson: Split

As for Stephen, he apologized in the moment during episode eight, but he also shared a message on social media once the episode aired.

"I hope I didn't ruin anyone's day by existing," he wrote on Instagram Stories in October 2024, "and if I did, I'm sorry you had to wake up this morning. I wish you didn't have to either. But I'll love you all the same."

Once Hannah and Nick embarked on life outside the pods, the season seven pair had their fair share of ups and downs—and disagreements—to say the least. (Let’s not forget: “I think you get treated as an equal when you star contributing like an equal.”)

And it all came to a head when Hannah decided they wouldn’t make it down the aisle. As for Nick, he called their breakup “one of the worst feelings of my life.”

Since then, Hannah has admitted the show forced her to do some self-introspection.

“I’ve learned a lot, I’ve learned there’s things I need to work on,” she said during an October 2024 episode of The Viall Files podcast. “For example, I am a very direct person. I know that but I think my delivery is rough. And I’ve learned that delivery is everything.”

Taylor Krause and Garrett Josemans: Married

A match made in science-based heaven (i.e. those serendipitous tattoos), season seven stars Taylor and Garrett clicked from the very beginning and just seemed destined to say, “I do.” Though they did hit a rough patch once Taylor found out he responded to an ex’s DM (according to Garrett, he confirmed he was engaged and shut it down), the rest is Love Is Blind history.

"I'm very grateful to have a life partner like my husband because no matter where we are in the world you make it feel like home," Taylor wrote in a November 2025 Instagram post marking their second anniversary. "I admire how much we have grown to build a life together and much of that has been because of you."

Yes, you read that right: Though Marissa and Ramses rose to become one of season seven's frontrunners of the couples who would make it, he ultimately called off their wedding after having second thoughts.

“We have a great future ahead of us, I want to marry you,” Marissa told her fiancé after a sit-down to which he responds, “I understand falling in love is a risk, I understand that.”

However, he noted their differences—which have included his stance on the military—may be too tough to work through. “After being married and seeing other marriages and hearing from other married people,” he added. “I just don’t think love alone is enough…I think there needs to be other things that are also working.”

As for Marissa, though she tried to navigate past their perspectives, once she confirmed it was over, she broke down into tears. “I don’t think you should’ve come to this experience,” she tells him. “How could I feel so sure? And you’re not? It sucks, I want you to choose me,” adding of their split, “This is the worst day of my life.”

She announced her marriage to former partner D. Johnson in May 2026.

Tyler Francis and Ashley Adionser: Divorced

Tyler and Ashley quickly became a fan-favorite couple after season seven viewers watched their relatively easy-going romance unfold. However, the couple hit a bump in the road once Tyler shared that he had three children, which Ashley referred to as his "sperm donor babies." (However, there’s online discourse over the extent of his involvement, which he has not addressed publicly).

By the October 2024 reunion episode, Ashley and Tyler were able to move past this fact and went on to not only reconnect—but in fact, become husband and wife.

“We started this journey two months ago and this changed our entire lives,” Tyler says while sitting alongside Ashley after their wedding. “Now, we get to spend the rest of our lives together.”

However, Ashley later shared that the pair had called it quits following over one year of marriage.

"After much reflection, I want to share that Tyler and I have been separated for several weeks and have now made the difficult decision to end our marriage," she told People in a January 2025 statement. "While I had hoped for mutual understanding and transparency in our relationship, it has become clear that our paths are no longer aligned, making it impossible for me to continue in this marriage."

Season seven stars Alex and Tim seemed to smooth over their major disagreement in Mexico by the time they got back home to Washington, D.C. In fact, Tim had an emotional meeting with Alex’s dad that seemed to cement their future.

However, after Alex met with Tim’s family, they got into yet another argument and Tim ended their engagement by telling Alex that he didn’t ever want to see her again. Since then, both have spoken out to defend themselves after the breakup, with Alex noting that their split was not “a mutual decision.”

The Taurid meteor shower could spawn dazzling fireballs in the coming weeks! Here's when and where to look.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Heads up stargazers! The Taurid meteor shower is upon us, bringing multiple peaks of activity that could see spectacular shooting stars and fireballs brighten November's sky. Here's where and when to look.

Every autumn, Earth plows through streams of debris left behind by Comet Encke, a 3-mile-wide (4.8-kilometer) ice body that orbits the sun once every 3.3 years.

These debris streams produce two branches of the Taurid meteor shower: The Southern Taurids, active from Sept. 20 to Nov. 20 and the Northern Taurids, active from Oct. 20 to Dec. 10.

As Earth plows through the debris streams, tiny particles slam into our atmosphere at 65,000 miles per hour (104,607 kilometers per hour), producing dazzling streaks of light across the night sky.

Both branches of the Taurid meteor shower appear to travel away from a point of origin — or radiant — located in the constellation Taurus, which rises in the southeastern sky during November evenings.

The Taurids are known for spawning brilliant fireball meteors, which can flare brighter than Venus as pebble-sized pieces of debris enter and burn up in the atmosphere.

The Southern Taurid shower features two distinct yearly peaks, the first of which occurred on Oct. 14. The second takes place overnight on Nov. 4-5 and is associated with an increase in fireball activity, when up to five meteors per hour could be seen blazing across the sky.

The Northern Taurid stream, meanwhile, is expected to peak overnight on Nov. 11-12 with the same predicted hourly rate of up to five meteors per hour streaking across the dark, near moonless sky.

Head out to a dark sky location around midnight on the night of the peaks, when the shower's radiant in the constellation Taurus is positioned high in the southeastern sky, maximizing the number of meteors that can be seen.

Remember not to stare directly at the radiant. Meteors seen close to the constellation Taurus strike our planet almost head-on, and so will have the shortest trails. Instead, pick out a patch of sky a little distance away, where the shooting stars will be at their most eye-catching as they skim through Earth's atmosphere.

Never use a telescope or binoculars to hunt for meteors, you want to take in as much of the sky as possible, not limit your field of view! And be sure to wrap up warm and allow 20-30 minutes for your eyes to adapt to the dark — a vital and often overlooked step for anyone hoping to catch even the faintest of meteors.

Check out our picks of the best cameras and lenses for astrophotography, along with our guide to capturing fast-moving meteors if you want to create a permanent memory of the next big shower.

Editor's Note: If you would like to share your photos of Taurid meteors with Space.com's readers, then please send your photo(s), comments, and your name and location to spacephotos@space.com.

#762. India increases growth forecast for fiscal year

India's Ministry of Finance has increased its growth forecasts for the current fiscal year. But it also warned about inflation, particularly for fuel and energy, amid continued instability in the Middle East.

India's Ministry of Finance expects India's economy to grow at a pace of 7.3% in the current fiscal year based on its latest assessment of current data, it said in its October economic review.

The estimate is a slight increase on the previous forecast of 7.1%.

India's current fiscal year, known as FY27, runs from April 1, 2026 to March 31, 2027.

The report contrasted these figures with global growth predictions of nearer 3%, saying "India's growth momentum, by comparison, has held firm."

The ministry said growth in various key indicators like energy consumption, port traffic, goods and services tax (GST) collections, and car sales had accelerated in the previous quarter.

However, the ministry also warned of continued inflationary pressure and pressure on the rupee currency, as well as downside risks from the El Nino weather phonemenon that could threaten soil moisture ahead of the winter sowing season.

It said that external factors like oil prices and "global uncertainties" — seemingly a reference at least in part to the instablity in the Middle East — continued to pressure the rupee's value and pose inflationary risks.

Consumer price inflation (CPI), the wholesale price index (WPI), food cost prices and fuel and power prices were all rising month for month, albeit at very different rates.

The CPI was up 5.54% year-on-year in September, but the WPI had risen more sharply at 11.39%. Food index inflation was up by 8% in rural areas, and a slightly more modest 7.18% in urban centers.

But, as in many other countries, fuel and power costs increases were in an entirely different league, at 25.85% inflation in September 2026 comapred to the same month a year earlier, prior to the outbreak of fighting in the Middle East.

Although it has been a comparatively slow decline, the rupee has been consistently losing value against the US dollar over the past five years, threatening the country's relative purchasing power internationally. This slide has picked up pace in the last 15 months or so.

But the ministry pointed to foreign exchange reserves worth some $721 billion and said that India was "well-positioned" to weather such risks and sustain its expansionary trajectory..

"We're talking about deploying 100 cubesats on a protect-and-defend mission for less than £100 million."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In May 2026, four Russian military satellites came close to ICEYE-X36, a private synthetic aperture radar satellite widely believed to be providing battlefield intelligence for Ukraine, in an apparently aggressive and risky "grey zone" maneuver that spooked many in the space industry.

Close enough to jam or interfere with the satellite's signal, blind it with a laser, fire a metal dart at it or, simply, force it to maneuver and burn fuel, the satellites' seemingly intimidatory behavior has increased the West's desire to develop defensive technology for satellites. In October 2026, it was reported that one of those same four Russian satellites passed within 500 meters (1,650 feet) of the same ICEYE satellite.

Now, U.K. startup Shield Space is racing to apply the lessons of drone warfare in Ukraine to develop swarms of up to 100 very small, low-cost, attritable drone-like autonomous spacecraft called cubesats. Released by a car-sized carrier in Earth orbit, these microwave-sized spacecraft will act as interceptors to protect Western satellites, and their deployment will mark a next step in the evolution of orbital warfare. Shield Space says that these space drones will use "effectors" like lasers or microwaves to defend Western satellites even if controllers lose contact with them.

"We're talking about deploying 100 cubesats on a protect-and-defend mission for less than £100 million [$134 million US], which is how [much] you would pay for one satellite previously," said Graeme Ritchie, co-founder and CEO of Shield Space.

Launched in 2023, NASA's civilian project Starling demonstrated that a swarm of four small satellites can cooperate and operate autonomously in space on a civilian science mission without relying heavily on real-time commands from ground control. But that seems like a far cry from the adversarial or defensive missions Shield Space and its competitors imagine. It is telling that the leading space powers appear not to have demonstrated swarm combat in space — although they tend to be reluctant to reveal their space warfare capabilities.

In the fourth quarter of 2027, Shield Space plans to take this next step in space warfare's evolution by demonstrating rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) with two very small spacecraft. This effort, named Project Broadsword, will launch on SpaceX's Transporter-21 rideshare mission. It will send up an 8U cubesat and a smaller 3U target craft, which Shield Space plans to maneuver from 100 kilometers (62 miles) apart to within 100 meters (330 feet) of each other and, through four stages of autonomy, from human-in-the-loop to "approximately" fully autonomous. (A cubesat unit, or U, is a cube that measures 10 cm, or about 4 inches, on a side.)

The gaps between a true satellite-defense capability and this demonstration appear to be great, in terms of the technological and practical challenges of squeezing propulsion and power systems, AI compute power, sensors, the lasers the swarm needs to communicate and weapon systems onto small, lightweight maneuvering satellites. But it is a gap that Shield Space believes it can bridge through the purchase of relatively cheap off-the-shelf technology rather than more expensive bespoke designs.

"Yes, it's a problem because of size, weight and power," Ritchie told Space.com. "We've had to totally innovate from scratch some elements of the mission… but we have only got roughly 100 cm by 100 cm [40 by 40 inches], so saving space or having systems that are already completely integrated is the main aim."

"We have commissioned EnduroSat to build us an autonomous 8U cubesat that has chemical propulsion and its own imagery-collecting capability, which we will put our software on," said Dan Molland, co-founder and CTO of Shield Space, "and which we will then use to conduct our RPO.

"The good thing about cubesats is they're very standardized and they're very off the shelf," he added. "There's always some level of adjusting you've got to do, but these cubesats are a lot more plug and play than more conventional platforms, which are usually all custom-built."

Yet to focus on the technical issues may be to miss the point. "It takes an extraordinary amount of data to train the models and algorithms to achieve a fully autonomous mission," said Ritchie, "and the problem [unlike in the Ukraine war] is that data is not readily available.

"We can train AI using synthetic data, but it's just not quite good enough for space. It's incredibly important to gather data from missions like this if we really want autonomous missions in the future."

There is also the complexity of the AI needed in a war-fighting system. "Starling is a really great example," Molland told Space.com. "With Starling, you're essentially just asking a guidance system to make sure you stay within a given range of this or that satellite… But if you are controlling a swarm to deliver [a] military mission, you have a much more complex set of questions."

It also comes with the challenge of ensuring that AI complies with any rules of engagement.

But Ritchie and Molland believe these technical challenges can be overcome, and they have an aggressive schedule of demonstrations planned that they think will prove it.

Bleddyn Bowen, associate professor of astropolitics at Durham University in the U.K. and author of the book "War in Space: Strategy, Spacepower, Geopolitics" (Edinburgh University Press, 2020), is more cautious about Shield Space's plans for the evolution of space warfare.

"They remind me of a late Cold War missile-defense scheme called Brilliant Pebbles," he told Space.com. "It was one of the more advanced research and development programs in the Strategic Defense Initiative."

The plan was to defend the U.S. against Soviet intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs) by using thousands of small autonomous orbiting interceptors to destroy them by collision.

"With enough investment, a lot is feasible," Bowen said.

"But you're looking at many years of development and testing," he added, "and finding someone to buy the system."

It is clear from Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine that the future of warfare includes swarms of low-cost autonomous drones — and Shield Space is already planning an aggressive schedule of missions to prove that this pattern applies to the final frontier as well.

According to Ritchie, the startup hopes to quickly go from the first RPO demonstration to testing two full-sized 16U cubesats. It will then move on to a full carrier of 10 such cubesats, and then to a "super carrier" of 10 carriers, which will be deployed across multiple orbits.

"We then get towards our future vision, which we call space-based carrier strike," said Ritchie. In this scenario, "responsive launch or pre-positioned carriers will give us an ability to protect and defend entire orbits, should you choose."

Editor's note: The original version of this story suggested that Shield Space may be working on "kinetic impact" satellite-defense techniques. The company says it is not doing this, so the story was updated to that effect at 10:45 a.m. ET on Nov. 5.

Mark is an award-winning freelance aviation and space journalist and author of the non-fiction book "N-4 DOWN: The Hunt for the Arctic airship Italia." He began writing for Space.com in 2026 and writes for a range of publications, from BBC Future to The Smithsonian’s Air and Space Quarterly and others. Space grabbed hold of Mark’s imagination when, as a child, he saw the opening scene of "Star Wars: A New Hope" for the first time and has never let go. Away from the final frontier, Mark can be found walking his dog along the country lanes of England’s Cotswolds.

#759. 'Star Trek' star Patrick Stewart dies age 86

The Shakespearean actor landed the role of a lifetime as "Star Trek" Captain Picard. He passed away at age 86.

For Star Trek fans, he was the legendary Captain Picard; the British actor and director Patrick Stewart, longtime member of the  Royal Shakespeare Company, died on Thursday at the age of 86 following a "brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, according to an official statement on his social media accounts.

In Los Angeles, California, far away from the small English village of Mirfield where he was born, Stewart achieved world fame. He was 47 years old when he landed the role of a lifetime in the legendary science fiction series Star Trek: Playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in "Star Trek: The Next Generation," he stepped into the shoes of the legendary Captain James T. Kirk, played by William Shatner.

Stewart brought a calm, measured and distinctly British presence that quickly made Picard a fan favorite and a cult figure in the Star Trek universe. He returned to the role decades later in the spin-off series "Star Trek: Picard," which ended in 2023, proving the character's enduring appeal.

As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, he led the crew of the starship Enterprise, a spaceship with the sizeable mission: "To explore strange new worlds. To seek out new life and new civilizations" — and most importantly, "to boldly go where no man has gone before!"

Stewart's interest in acting was sparked in the early 1950s when a teacher asked him to recite a work by Shakespeare. His passion for Shakespeare stayed with him until the end.

His parents were far removed from the glamor of the theatrical world. His father was a highly respected officer in the British Army during World War II, but at home, he was an abusive husband, and young Patrick had to helplessly witness repeated violence against his mother. Stewart wrote about his experiences with domestic violence in The Guardian in 2009. The stage, he confessed there, seemed to him "a far safer place" than reality; he saw acting as a way to escape his home life.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Patrick began acting at the age of 12. At 16, he left school early and, thanks to a scholarship, studied acting in Bristol, England. Along the way, he worked as a journalist. In 1965, he became an official member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, and remained with the theather company from 1966 to 1982. Such was his passion for the great English playwright and lyricist that he even shared his sonnets on his Twitter account during the 2020 coronavirus pandemic.

Stewart dazzled the theater world with his own stage adaptation of Charles Dickens' 1843 tale "A Christmas Carol." He played more than 30 roles himself. After its 1987 premiere in Stewart's hometown of Mirfield, the one-man show became a critics' favorite and a long-running hit on Broadway in New York.

In the same year,  Stewart went from being a stage actor to an international TV star. Star Trek producer Robert Justman offered him the role of Captain Jean-Luc Picard, one of the main characters in a new edition of the popular TV series "Star Trek: The Next Generation."

The successful Shakespearean hesitated. Until then, he had never worked in Hollywood. But his agent encouraged him to accept the role, Stewart recalled in a 2020 interview with the German newspaper Die Welt. "You can accept the offer as a start for now. It won't be a big deal, you can't revive a series as iconic as Star Trek anyway."

But his agent was to be proven wrong: Stewart led the Starship Enterprise through its galactic adventures for seven seasons and four full-length feature films. The TV series had astronomical success on Earth in a very short time. At first, the producers were at odds as to whether Stewart's British accent could really fit the role of commander of a US starship in the 24th century, but it soon became impossible to imagine the series without the subtly diplomatic Captain Picard, who often quoted Shakespeare while at the helm. It seemed as if all the time he had spent as a Shakespearean actor had prepared him to command the Enterprise, Stewart once remarked with a wink. When the cult series ended in 1994, he had ruled out ever returning to the Enterprise's command center.

In 2010, the actor was knighted by the Queen of England. Stewart considered it the greatest honor of his career to stand alongside acting greats such as Sir Laurence Olivier and Sir Alec Guinness.

Beyond the screen, Stewart has long used his voice for social and human rights causes. In recent years, he has drawn attention to issues such as violence against women, age discrimination and the protection of children.

In a June 2020 interview, "Playboy" asked the New York resident whether he was considering retiring from acting. "Never! That would mean giving up my life," replied Stewart, who was approaching his 80th birthday at the time. He was filming the second of three seasons of "Star Trek: Picard." The series ends with a final episode in which the retired Starfleet admiral makes his last appearance. In the series, Picard retires to his family vineyard in France but is drawn back into space to confront new threats to the Federation.

This series also showcases Stewart's affection for his pit bull, Ginger. In "Star Trek: Picard," Picard also has a pit bull, a loyal four-legged companion named Number One — a deliberate reference to Stewart's real-life love of the breed. For his efforts to combat prejudice against pit bulls and to support their adoption, Stewart was honored by the US animal welfare organization ASPCA, among others.

In 2024, he published his memoir "Making it So." In it, he recounts his passion for theater and his love of Shakespeare.

Now, at the age of 86, the British actor has finally departed for another galaxy. Farewell, Patrick Stewart!

#758. ‘Mathematics is more than a mechanical process’ — why I think the field will survive OpenAI’s disruption

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Ursula Martin is an emeritus professor at the Mathematical Institute, University of Oxford, UK.

In early October, the artificial-intelligence firm OpenAI posted more than 700 AI-generated mathematical manuscripts on an online public repository. The arguments — if found to be correct after verification — contain an extraordinary trove of new mathematical knowledge. The reaction to these developments from the maths community has ranged from exhilaration to despair. Some researchers worry they have spent their lifetimes attempting to solve problems and their work might now suddenly seem meaningless. Others have expressed concern about the negative impact on young colleagues who are entering the field during a period of flux. And there’s been widespread anger at the manner in which AI companies are releasing such findings.

As one of the authors of the Leiden Declaration on Artificial Intelligence and Mathematics, which was published in June, I think some of the field’s concerns over OpenAI’s approach to announcing its discoveries could have been anticipated. In our declaration, we did not oppose the use of AI but put forwards several practical safeguards. These included the need for clear citation policies, precise disclosures on how AI is used and a renewed commitment to the long-standing expectation that all arguments made in a maths proof should be independently verifiable and answerable by a human author. Some AI companies have agreed to follow the declaration. OpenAI has not.

Mathematicians are developing rules for AI use — other fields should follow

Mathematicians are developing rules for AI use — other fields should follow

Now that mathematicians have started analysing the AI-assisted proofs, it’s clear that many of the 700 preprints are presented in a sloppy, rough-and-ready style, making them hard to understand. The inner workings of OpenAI’s closed models are unknown, and there is also no human author named who might take responsibility for explaining or correcting the content if flaws emerge. It will take mathematicians a lot of time and effort to check the work in the preprints and rewrite it in a professional format that is suitable for judgement by peer reviewers. Unsurprisingly, many mathematicians are unenthusiastic about clearing up OpenAI’s mess, however exciting the underlying mathematics might be.

So, what does this mean for the future of mathematics? Creatively rethinking how the field must evolve will require action at every level. Outstanding leadership by individuals such as mathematician Terence Tao, and grassroots initiatives such as the Leiden declaration, need to be complemented with high-level engagement from stakeholder institutions such as the International Mathematical Union. It would be a disservice to the field if AI companies are allowed to set the norms on how to do mathematics without wide-ranging input from academics.

#757. Scientists smash oxygen nuclei to recreate matter from the Big Bang

New findings from the STAR experiment at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) suggest that scientists can recreate an extraordinary form of matter from the earliest moments of the universe using surprisingly small atomic collisions. By smashing oxygen nuclei together at nearly the speed of light, researchers have uncovered strong evidence of quark-gluon plasma (QGP), an extremely hot and dense state of matter that existed shortly after the Big Bang.

The findings, published in Physical Review Letters, reveal that high-energy streams of particles lose energy as they travel through the material created by these collisions. This effect, called jet quenching, provides an important clue that quark-gluon plasma has formed.

Scientists have previously observed jet quenching in collisions involving much larger atomic nuclei at RHIC, a U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Office of Science User Facility that operated at Brookhaven National Laboratory from 2000 until 2026. The same effect has also been detected in oxygen collisions at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the European Particle Physics Laboratory.

What makes the new RHIC findings especially significant is that the oxygen collisions occurred at substantially lower energies. The results establish a new lower boundary for the conditions known to produce quark-gluon plasma in this small collision system, helping scientists narrow down what it takes to create matter resembling that of the infant universe.

"The QGP is believed to be the form of matter that filled the early universe -- before the protons and neutrons that make up today's atoms formed. Understanding its properties is essential for uncovering how the early universe evolved in its first microseconds," said Li Yi, a professor of physics at Shandong University who oversaw the STAR analysis.

"One of the most powerful ways scientists study the QGP is by identifying where its signatures appear -- and just as importantly, where these signatures turn off," she said.

Rongrong Ma, a STAR physicist at Brookhaven Lab, explained why investigating smaller collisions is so valuable.

"This analysis is pushing the boundaries to an extreme case to help us learn something about this jet quenching phenomenon and the conditions needed to generate a QGP."

How Scientists Recreate Matter From the Early Universe

RHIC was designed specifically to produce and investigate quark-gluon plasma. Traditionally, researchers have accomplished this by accelerating gold nuclei to enormous speeds and crashing them into one another.

Each gold nucleus contains 79 protons and 118 neutrons. When two such nuclei collide with sufficient energy, the boundaries of their protons and neutrons effectively break down, releasing the quarks and gluons inside them. The tremendous energy of the impact also generates thousands of additional quarks and gluons through the conversion of energy into matter, as described by Einstein's famous equation, E=mc2.

The result is a fleeting droplet of primordial matter. It is smaller than an atomic nucleus and survives for less than a billionth of a billionth of a second. Almost immediately, the quarks and gluons recombine into more familiar particles.

Because this exotic substance disappears so quickly, scientists cannot examine it directly. Instead, they use enormous instruments such as the STAR detector to analyze the particles that emerge from the collision.

One particularly revealing clue comes from particles that escape with less energy than expected. Their reduced energy suggests they interacted with the dense mixture of quarks and gluons before escaping.

Researchers pay special attention to jets, which are narrow sprays of extremely energetic particles. These often originate when a quark or gluon from one nucleus strikes a quark or gluon from another, sending two particle jets traveling in opposite directions.

If these paired jets, known as "di-jets," form near the edge of the collision region, one may have to travel farther through the plasma than the other. Comparing their behavior allows scientists to investigate how the surrounding material drains energy from particles passing through it.

Yi offered a familiar comparison to explain the process.

"You can think of it like shooting a bullet through, say, water," Yi said. "Because of the resistance, the bullet will slow down. It's the same thing with these high-energy particles. When they go through the QGP, they will lose energy."

For decades, RHIC experiments have provided clear evidence of jet quenching in collisions between gold nuclei. The effect is especially noticeable in jets that travel longer distances through the newly created matter.

Scientists believe these particles lose more energy because they encounter more quarks and gluons before escaping. Jets originating closer to the outer boundary generally pass through less material and experience fewer interactions.

These measurements helped establish that RHIC was successfully producing quark-gluon plasma. Additional evidence came from several other experiments, including an unexpected discovery about how the resulting matter behaves.

Scientists observed that relatively low-energy particles emerging from gold collisions moved collectively, following coordinated patterns. This behavior indicated that the plasma flowed almost like a perfect liquid, with extraordinarily little viscosity or internal resistance.

The discovery was a major surprise when researchers first identified it. Collective flow has since become another important "smoking gun" signature of quark-gluon plasma.

Can Tiny Atomic Collisions Create Primordial Matter?

After establishing these signatures in collisions involving large nuclei, physicists began finding similar collective motion in much smaller systems.

Experiments at the LHC, followed by studies at RHIC, detected collective flow when tiny projectiles such as protons, deuterons, and helium-3 nuclei struck much larger gold or lead nuclei. Researchers at the LHC even observed comparable flow patterns in collisions between individual protons.

These results raised a major question. Did the coordinated particle motion mean that these much smaller collisions were also producing quark-gluon plasma, or could another mechanism explain the observations?

Scientists needed a more definitive sign.

"The next natural question is: Can you see jet quenching, the other key signature that QGP is formed, in these very small collision systems?" asked Brookhaven's Ma. "We haven't seen any unambiguous signal, so it's still kind of under debate in these small systems. We want to search for the smallest system where we can still see an unambiguous jet-quenching signal," he said.

To investigate, researchers turned to collisions between oxygen nuclei.

An oxygen nucleus contains just eight protons and eight neutrons, making it far smaller than the gold nuclei typically used in RHIC experiments. Oxygen nuclei also have a relatively symmetrical, spherical shape, which makes the geometry of their collisions easier to analyze.

"That means we can more easily look for signs of asymmetric quenching of di-jets produced close to the edge of the circular interaction region in head-on collisions," said Maowu Nie, an associate professor at Shandong University who contributed to the research.

The scientists could also examine how the outcome changed depending on whether the oxygen nuclei collided directly or merely grazed one another.

"We can also compare how jets behave in head-on central collisions -- those that produce the most particles and therefore have the highest likelihood of making a QGP -- with collisions where the two oxygen nuclei barely strike each other, which aren't expected to generate a QGP."

Nie explained that these grazing collisions are recognizable because they generate far fewer particles than direct impacts.

Oxygen Collisions Reveal a 20% Suppression

To search for jet quenching, the researchers developed an analysis that identifies concentrated streams of high-energy particles and measures how many emerge above a selected energy threshold.

"Our measurements are essentially counting experiments," said Sijie Zhang, who conducted the research for her master's thesis under Yi and Nie at Shandong University and is now pursuing a Ph.D. at Yale University.

"We have an algorithm that finds the collimated groups of high-energy particles, the jets, and we count how many of these particles above a certain energy threshold come out."

Yang He, a former Ph.D. student at Shandong University who developed the analysis framework and now studies oxygen collisions at the LHC, described how the team used different collision types to identify energy loss.

"We compare what we see in back-to-back jets produced near the edge of the system, and we compare what we see in head-on collisions with the counts in non-central collisions where we don't expect to see quenching."

The team analyzed STAR measurements from oxygen collisions conducted at RHIC in 2021, at a collision energy of 200 billion electron volts (GeV).

The results revealed a 20% suppression of high-energy particles associated with jet quenching.

Although this suppression was smaller than what physicists typically measure in gold collisions, that difference was expected because oxygen collisions generate much smaller systems.

Crucially, the observed effect was still strong enough to provide clear evidence that quark-gluon plasma had formed.

Comparing Big Bang Matter at Different Energies

Oxygen offers scientists another important advantage. Apart from proton-proton collisions, it is the only nuclear species that has been investigated in collisions at both RHIC and the LHC.

That gives researchers an unusual opportunity to make an "apples-to-apples" comparison between two facilities operating at very different collision energies.

The LHC carried out its first oxygen collisions in 2025. According to results reported by CERN, those experiments revealed both collective flow and jet quenching, providing additional indications that quark-gluon plasma can form in relatively small nuclear collisions.

However, the LHC operated at collision energies exceeding 5,000 GeV, far above the 200 GeV used in the RHIC measurements.

"With a higher energy collision, it's more likely to create more and more quarks and gluons and a hotter, denser QGP system," Yi said. "That means the jet quenching signal, if it's there, should be bigger at LHC compared to RHIC."

While higher energies make it easier to create the hot, dense conditions needed for quark-gluon plasma, lower-energy experiments may be more useful for determining precisely when those conditions are no longer sufficient.

By reducing the collision energy and using smaller nuclei, physicists can approach the threshold at which the distinctive signatures of primordial matter disappear.

"We are pushing the boundaries in two ways to explore the minimal conditions for creating a QGP, both in terms of the nucleus size by looking at these small oxygen-oxygen collisions, but also by looking at data from lower collision energies -- and we still see this crucial QGP signature. That's a unique feature of our measurement," Ma said.

New Experiments Could Reveal the Limits of Primordial Matter

Although RHIC has now completed its operations, scientists still have additional oxygen collision data to investigate.

During the collider's final experimental run, researchers collected measurements using both STAR and sPHENIX, RHIC's newest detector. The facility concluded its operations with oxygen collisions recorded by both instruments on February 6, 2026.

These remaining datasets could provide further insights into how small a collision system can become, and how low its energy can fall, before quark-gluon plasma can no longer form.

Understanding those limits may help physicists piece together the behavior of matter during the first microseconds of the universe, when quarks and gluons had not yet combined into the protons and neutrons that make up ordinary atoms today.

The research received financial support from the DOE Office of Science, the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF), and additional international agencies and organizations identified in the scientific publication.

The researchers also used the Open Science Grid, which receives direct support from NSF, along with computing resources at Brookhaven Lab's Scientific Data and Computing Facilities and the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC), a DOE Office of Science User Facility located at DOE's Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

Students gathered under the stars in Hawaii recently to explore the awesome nature of the night sky together.

From Oct. 19 to Oct. 22, more than 1,400 students on the Big Island of Hawaii gathered for the Journey Through the Universe event to explore astronomy together.

The Journey Through the Universe program is currently in its 23rd year. It was originally developed by the National Center for Earth and Space Science Education (NCESSE) and later introduced in Hawaii by the international Gemini Observatory, a program within the U.S. National Science Foundation's NOIRLab (National Optical-Infrared Astronomy Research Laboratory) that works with the Department of Education Hilo-Waiākea.

The program aims to introduce students in the Hilo-Waiākea public school system to astronomy as well as the incredible science that happens across Hawaii. The students who participate range from preschoolers to seniors in high school, so the program introduces some students to astronomy and helps others explore possible careers in STEM fields.

This year, the program brought in 19 volunteer educators from scientific institutions like Maunakea Observatories and supported hands-on activities and lessons that went from the classroom to under the Milky Way.

This image shows a growing love for astronomy in progress. From the red glow of a skywatching night (red light doesn't interfere with our ability to see at night like white light does) to the scattered telescopes and students standing under the stars, this scene paints a larger picture.

This is just one program, but in bringing together volunteers, educators, scientists and students, the program has created an incredible and enduring learning experience.

Whether or not students walk away wanting to pursue a career in STEM, this incredible immersion in astronomy can help to foster a lifelong appreciation for science and nature. It's always a great idea to gather under the stars and explore together.
